explanation.summary: A Cloud KMS key's rotation period creates a new primary version on schedule, under the customer's control, and Compute Engine uses it for new encryption.

option_breakdown.A: Google-managed keys are rotated by Google; the customer has no rotation setting to control.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. A Cloud KMS key's rotation period creates a new primary version on schedule, under the customer's control, and Compute Engine uses it for new encryption.
option_breakdown.C: CSEK has no schedule: you would rotate and supply raw keys yourself on every call.
option_breakdown.D: Re-creating disks is disruptive and still leaves the key under Google's control.

questions.title: Every externally exposed Service in a cluster
questions.summary: kubectl get services --all-namespaces lists every Service with its type and external IP.
questions.question: During a security review, you must list every Kubernetes Service in a GKE cluster that has an external IP address, whatever namespace it is in. What should you list?

options.A: The Pods, with their IP addresses and nodes.
options.B: The Services in every namespace.
options.C: The GKE cluster's own description.
options.D: The nodes, with their external IP addresses.

explanation.summary: Services carry the TYPE and EXTERNAL-IP columns; --all-namespaces (-A) removes the namespace scope. LoadBalancer Services with an address in EXTERNAL-IP are the ones exposed.

option_breakdown.A: Pod listings show Pod IPs and nodes, not how workloads are exposed.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. kubectl get services --all-namespaces lists Services across every namespace with their external IPs.
option_breakdown.C: The cluster description covers cluster settings, not the Services inside it.
option_breakdown.D: Node external IPs are not how applications are exposed and miss every load balancer.

questions.title: Which node and node pool each Pod runs on
questions.summary: kubectl get pods -o wide shows each Pod's node; node labels show the node pool.
questions.question: You need to know which node each Pod of the 'payments' namespace is running on, and which node pool those nodes belong to. What should you run?

options.A: A description of the payments Deployment.
options.B: The cluster's list of node pools.
options.C: Pods with their nodes, then nodes with their pool label.
options.D: The Pods' current resource usage.

explanation.summary: The wide output adds a NODE column per Pod; GKE labels every node with cloud.google.com/gke-nodepool, which -L displays as a column. Together they map Pods to nodes to pools.

option_breakdown.A: A Deployment description shows the template and rollout, not placement per Pod.
option_breakdown.B: Lists pools but not which Pods run on their nodes.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. kubectl get pods -o wide gives each Pod's node, and kubectl get nodes -L cloud.google.com/gke-nodepool gives each node's pool.
option_breakdown.D: Shows resource usage, not placement.

explanation.gcloud_command:
kubectl get pods -n payments -o wide
kubectl get nodes -L cloud.google.com/gke-nodepool

questions.title: An Autopilot Pod killed for memory
questions.summary: Autopilot provisions capacity from each container's requests; raise the memory request to give the Pod more.
questions.question: A container on a GKE Autopilot cluster is repeatedly OOMKilled. Its manifest sets a memory request of 512Mi and no other resource values. The application genuinely needs about 1.5 GiB. What should you change?

options.A: Add a node pool with larger machines to the cluster.
options.B: Remove the memory request so Autopilot can allocate memory dynamically.
options.C: Enable the cluster autoscaler on the Autopilot cluster.
options.D: Raise the container's memory request to about 1.5Gi.

explanation.summary: Autopilot sizes capacity, and bills, from Pod resource requests, and applies limits based on them. The fix is a request that matches real usage. Node pools and the cluster autoscaler are managed by Google in Autopilot.

option_breakdown.A: Autopilot manages nodes; you do not add node pools.
option_breakdown.B: Without a request Autopilot applies a small default, which makes the problem worse.
option_breakdown.C: Node scaling is automatic in Autopilot and is not the constraint here.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. The request is what Autopilot allocates and bills.

questions.title: A canary split for a Cloud Run function
questions.summary: Cloud Run functions are Cloud Run services, so traffic is split between their revisions with update-traffic.
questions.question: A function deployed with `gcloud functions deploy` (Cloud Run functions) has a new version. You want 20% of requests to reach the new revision and 80% the previous one. What should you do?

options.A: Deploy the new version as a second function and weight the two URLs in Cloud DNS.
options.B: Put both versions behind an external Application Load Balancer with weighted backends.
options.C: Delete the old revision so the platform shifts traffic gradually by itself.
options.D: Split traffic between the function's revisions.

explanation.summary: A Cloud Run function is deployed as a Cloud Run service, so it has revisions and supports percentage traffic splits and tags exactly like any other Cloud Run service.

option_breakdown.A: DNS weighting is coarse, cached by clients, and doubles what you operate.
option_breakdown.B: A load balancer is unnecessary; the service already splits traffic between revisions.
option_breakdown.C: Deleting the previous revision removes the rollback target and does not create a gradual split.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Revision-level percentages on the underlying Cloud Run service.

questions.title: Weighted routing between two versions on GKE
questions.summary: With the Gateway API, an HTTPRoute's backendRefs weights split traffic between Services.
questions.question: On GKE, version 1 and version 2 of an application run as separate Deployments, each behind its own Service, exposed through the Gateway API. You want 90% of requests on v1 and 10% on v2. What should you change?

options.A: Scale v1 to nine replicas and v2 to one, relying on one Service selecting both.
options.B: Weights of 90 and 10 on the HTTPRoute's two backends.
options.C: Create a second Gateway for v2 and give users its IP address.
options.D: Add a HorizontalPodAutoscaler to v2 with a 10% CPU target.

explanation.summary: An HTTPRoute can reference several backend Services with weights, and GKE's Gateway controller programs the load balancer to split traffic accordingly — independent of replica counts.

option_breakdown.A: Replica ratios give only approximate splits and couple capacity to routing.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Precise, declarative weights at the load balancer.
option_breakdown.C: A separate entry point means clients choose the version, not a percentage split.
option_breakdown.D: An autoscaler changes replica counts; it does not route traffic.

explanation.gcloud_command: kubectl apply -f route.yaml   # HTTPRoute backendRefs: [{name: app-v1, weight: 90}, {name: app-v2, weight: 10}]

questions.title: Adding a GPU to an existing VM
questions.summary: Attaching a GPU requires the VM to be stopped, host maintenance set to TERMINATE, and the GPU offered in its zone.
questions.question: An existing N1 VM needs an NVIDIA T4 attached for an inference workload. What must be true for the change to succeed?

options.A: It is stopped, set to terminate on maintenance, and T4s exist in its zone.
options.B: It keeps running; GPUs hot-plug and the maintenance policy can stay.
options.C: It is converted to Spot, since GPUs are offered only as Spot capacity.
options.D: It is recreated in any region, since GPUs are global resources.

explanation.summary: GPUs cannot live-migrate, so an instance with GPUs must use onHostMaintenance=TERMINATE. The accelerator is attached while the VM is stopped, and only GPU models offered in the VM's zone (and compatible with its machine series) can be attached.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. All three conditions apply to attaching a GPU to an existing instance.
option_breakdown.B: GPUs are not hot-plugged, and live migration is not supported for them.
option_breakdown.C: GPUs are available on standard as well as Spot provisioning.
option_breakdown.D: Accelerators are zonal; availability must be checked per zone.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud compute instances stop infer-1 --zone=ZONE
gcloud compute instances set-scheduling infer-1 --zone=ZONE --maintenance-policy=TERMINATE
gcloud compute instances set-machine-type ...   # or edit the instance to add the accelerator, then start

questions.title: Running a training Pod on TPUs in GKE
questions.summary: In GKE, TPUs come from a TPU node pool (or an Autopilot TPU compute class) and Pods request google.com/tpu.
questions.question: A training job in a GKE Standard cluster must run on Cloud TPU chips. What should you do?

options.A: Attach a TPU to one existing node as an accelerator.
options.B: Raise the Pod's CPU request until it lands on TPU hardware.
options.C: Add a TPU node pool, and have the Pod request google.com/tpu.
options.D: Install TPU drivers in the container image.

explanation.summary: TPUs are provisioned as TPU slice node pools (in Autopilot, through a TPU compute class). Workloads select the TPU type and topology with node selectors and request google.com/tpu so the scheduler places them there.

option_breakdown.A: TPUs come with TPU machine types; they can't be attached to an ordinary node.
option_breakdown.B: CPU requests never cause TPU scheduling.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. A TPU node pool with the right TPU version and topology, plus a Pod that selects it and requests google.com/tpu, is how GKE schedules work onto TPUs.
option_breakdown.D: TPUs exist only on TPU machine types; drivers alone do not create hardware.

questions.title: Least privilege for a deployed agent's tools
questions.summary: An agent on Agent Runtime acts through its service identity; grant that identity only the roles its tools need.
questions.question: An agent deployed to Agent Runtime has a tool that queries one BigQuery dataset. It fails with a permission error. The agent must not be able to touch any other data. What should you do?

options.A: Data Viewer on that dataset and Job User on the project, for its identity.
options.B: Grant roles/editor to the agent's service identity so every tool works.
options.C: Embed a service account key with BigQuery Admin in the agent's code.
options.D: Grant BigQuery Data Viewer on the dataset to every user who chats with the agent.

explanation.summary: Agent Runtime runs each agent with a service identity, and every tool call is authorised as that identity. Least privilege means binding exactly the data-read role on the dataset and the job-creation role needed to run queries.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Exactly the permissions the tool needs, on the narrowest scope.
option_breakdown.B: Editor spans every service and makes any prompt injection far more damaging.
option_breakdown.C: Keys are long-lived secrets and unnecessary when the runtime provides an identity.
option_breakdown.D: Tool calls do not run as the chatting user, and this grants data to many people.

questions.title: Finding the slow step inside an agent's answer
questions.summary: Agent Runtime emits traces, so Cloud Trace shows which model or tool call made an answer slow.
questions.question: Users report that an agent deployed to Agent Runtime sometimes takes 20 seconds to answer. You need to know whether the time goes to the model or to one of its three tool calls. What should you use?

options.A: Cloud Profiler attached to the agent's container.
options.B: The billing export, comparing model token costs per day.
options.C: Personalized Service Health for the Agent Platform service.
options.D: Cloud Trace, reading the latency of each span.

explanation.summary: Agent Runtime integrates with Cloud Trace: each request produces a trace whose spans cover model calls and tool invocations, so the slow step is visible directly.

option_breakdown.A: Profiler attributes CPU inside a process; it does not break a request into model and tool calls.
option_breakdown.B: Costs say nothing about latency of individual requests.
option_breakdown.C: Service Health reports Google incidents, not your agent's internal timing.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Per-span latency for model and tool calls.

explanation.gcloud_command: # Console > Trace Explorer, filtered on the agent's service name

questions.title: Notebook VMs left running all weekend
questions.summary: Workbench instances support idle shutdown, which stops the VM after a period of inactivity.
questions.question: Data scientists use Agent Platform Workbench instances (formerly Vertex AI Workbench) with GPUs and often leave them running over the weekend. You want idle notebooks to stop costing compute without deleting them. What should you configure?

options.A: A budget alert on the project at 90% of the monthly amount.
options.B: Delete-on-idle through an object lifecycle rule.
options.C: Idle shutdown on the Workbench instances.
options.D: A Cloud Scheduler job that deletes every instance on Friday evening.

explanation.summary: Idle shutdown stops a Workbench instance after it has been idle for the configured time. The VM, its disk and notebooks remain and can be started again; compute and GPU charges stop.

option_breakdown.A: A budget alert notifies; it stops nothing.
option_breakdown.B: Lifecycle rules apply to Cloud Storage objects, not VMs.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Stops idle instances while keeping their disks and notebooks.
option_breakdown.D: Deleting instances destroys work and configuration.

questions.title: Running a BigQuery notebook every night
questions.summary: BigQuery Studio notebooks (Colab Enterprise) can be scheduled to run on a runtime template.
questions.question: An analyst has a notebook in BigQuery Studio that refreshes a set of tables. It must run every night at 02:00 without anyone opening it, on a machine type an administrator has approved. What should you do?

options.A: Schedule the notebook in BigQuery Studio, using an approved runtime template.
options.B: Export the notebook to a VM and run it with cron.
options.C: Convert every cell into a separate scheduled query.
options.D: Leave a Workbench instance running with the notebook open.

explanation.summary: BigQuery notebooks run on Colab Enterprise runtimes defined by runtime templates, and a notebook can be scheduled directly. The schedule runs it serverlessly at the chosen time.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Native scheduling on a governed runtime.
option_breakdown.B: Moving it to a VM adds infrastructure to run and patch.
option_breakdown.C: Python and visualisation cells cannot become scheduled queries, and the logic would be split apart.
option_breakdown.D: An always-on instance costs money continuously and still needs someone to trigger the run.

explanation.gcloud_command: # BigQuery Studio > notebook > Schedule   (choose the runtime template and the frequency)

questions.title: Standard dev environments with private network access
questions.summary: Cloud Workstations run in a cluster on your VPC, with configurations that fix the image, machine and timeouts.
questions.question: Developers must work from standardised environments with the team's tools preinstalled, reach a Cloud SQL instance that has only a private IP, and keep source code off their laptops. How should you set up Cloud Workstations?

options.A: Give each developer a Compute Engine VM with an external IP and a desktop environment.
options.B: A workstation cluster in the VPC, with a configuration on a custom image.
options.C: Use Cloud Shell for everyone, installing tools into each person's home directory.
options.D: Create one shared workstation that all developers log in to.

explanation.summary: A workstation cluster places workstations in a VPC subnet, so they reach private resources. A workstation configuration sets the container image (tools preinstalled, stored in Artifact Registry), machine type, disk and idle timeouts for every developer's workstation.

option_breakdown.A: Hand-built VMs drift, expose external IPs and are not managed development environments.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Private networking from the cluster; standard tooling from the configuration's image.
option_breakdown.C: Cloud Shell has no VPC placement and a small home directory; tools per user drift.
option_breakdown.D: Shared environments break per-developer isolation and attribution.

questions.title: Running instances across every zone, as a table
questions.summary: gcloud compute instances list covers all zones; --filter and --format shape the result.
questions.question: Before a maintenance window, the on-call engineer at Glenmore Retail needs a single list of only the running Compute Engine VMs in the current project, across all zones, showing each VM's name, zone and machine type. What should the engineer run?

options.A: A describe of each instance, one at a time.
options.B: An instance list per zone, combined by hand.
options.C: A list of the project's managed instance groups.
options.D: One instance list, with a status filter and a table format.

explanation.summary: instances list already spans every zone unless restricted. --filter selects on any field, and --format chooses the columns.

option_breakdown.A: describe shows one named instance at a time, which is slow and needs the names first.
option_breakdown.B: It works, but instances list already covers every zone by default.
option_breakdown.C: Instance groups miss standalone VMs and don't show each VM's status.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. gcloud compute instances list --filter='status=RUNNING' --format='table(name,zone,machineType)' covers every zone in one call.

questions.title: Reading recent rows from Bigtable by key prefix
questions.summary: cbt read with a prefix reads rows whose keys start with a device ID.
questions.question: Bigtable row keys have the form `deviceId#reverseTimestamp`. You need to inspect the most recent five rows for device `pump-17` from the command line. What should you run?

options.A: A cbt read with a row-key prefix and a count.
options.B: A BigQuery query filtering on the device column.
options.C: A describe of the Bigtable instance.
options.D: A Spanner SQL query against the table.

explanation.summary: cbt is Bigtable's command-line tool. Reading with a key prefix scans only that device's rows, and because the timestamp is reversed, the first rows returned are the newest.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. A prefix read, newest first thanks to the reversed timestamp.
option_breakdown.B: BigQuery does not query Bigtable unless an external table is defined, and not with this syntax.
option_breakdown.C: Describing an instance shows its configuration, not table rows.
option_breakdown.D: Spanner commands do not work against Bigtable.

questions.title: An ad-hoc SQL query against a Spanner database
questions.summary: gcloud spanner databases execute-sql runs SQL against a Spanner database from the command line.
questions.question: You need to run a quick SQL query against the `orders` database in the Spanner instance `prod` from Cloud Shell, without installing a client. What should you run?

options.A: bq query, with standard SQL
options.B: gcloud sql connect to the instance
options.C: gcloud spanner databases execute-sql
options.D: cbt count on the table

explanation.summary: execute-sql sends a SQL statement to a Spanner database and prints the result. (The console's Spanner Studio does the same interactively.)

option_breakdown.A: bq targets BigQuery, not Spanner.
option_breakdown.B: gcloud sql connect is for Cloud SQL instances.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Spanner's own command-line query path.
option_breakdown.D: cbt is for Bigtable.

explanation.gcloud_command: gcloud spanner databases execute-sql orders --instance=prod --sql='SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Orders'

questions.title: Estimating a storage bill that includes retrieval
questions.summary: The Pricing Calculator models storage, operations and retrieval together for a planned configuration.
questions.question: Before approving a design, finance wants a monthly estimate for keeping 200 TB in Coldline Storage, of which about 5% is read back each month. Nothing is deployed yet. What should you do?

options.A: Create the bucket, upload a sample, and read the next invoice.
options.B: Model storage, operations and retrieval in the Pricing Calculator.
options.C: Multiply 200 TB by the Coldline per-GB storage price and report that figure.
options.D: Create a budget of the expected amount and read its forecast.

explanation.summary: The Pricing Calculator estimates planned resources, including the retrieval fees and operation charges that colder classes add. Counting only the per-GB storage price understates the cost of reading data back.

option_breakdown.A: Deploying first is slow and costly, and a sample does not show the real bill.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Storage, operations and retrieval together, before anything exists.
option_breakdown.C: Coldline charges for retrieval and operations as well; ignoring them understates the estimate.
option_breakdown.D: Budgets forecast from actual spend, and there is no spend yet.

explanation.gcloud_command: # https://cloud.google.com/products/calculator > Cloud Storage > Coldline, 200 TB, retrieval 10 TB/month

questions.title: Scheduled Firestore backups kept for weeks
questions.summary: Firestore backup schedules take daily or weekly backups; restores create a new database.
questions.question: A Firestore database needs a daily backup kept for 14 weeks, and the team must be able to restore any of those backups without affecting the live database. What should you configure?

options.A: Point-in-time recovery, which keeps versions for 14 weeks.
options.B: A nightly export from the application into a bucket it also serves traffic from.
options.C: Firestore in multi-region mode, which keeps historical copies automatically.
options.D: A daily Firestore backup schedule with 14-week retention.

explanation.summary: Firestore scheduled backups run daily or weekly with a retention of up to 14 weeks. A restore always creates a new database from the backup, leaving the live one untouched.

option_breakdown.A: Point-in-time recovery covers a short recent window (about seven days), not 14 weeks.
option_breakdown.B: Application-driven exports are fragile and mix backup files with serving data.
option_breakdown.C: Multi-region replication provides availability, not history.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Managed schedule, managed retention, restore to a new database.

questions.title: Recovering an AlloyDB cluster to ten minutes ago
questions.summary: AlloyDB continuous backup allows point-in-time recovery into a new cluster.
questions.question: A bad deployment corrupted data in an AlloyDB for PostgreSQL cluster ten minutes ago. Continuous backup and recovery is enabled with its default settings. How do you get the data as it was just before the deployment?

options.A: A point-in-time restore from continuous backup, into a new cluster.
options.B: Promote the read pool instance, which lags the primary by ten minutes.
options.C: Restore last night's on-demand backup over the running cluster.
options.D: Export the database and remove the corrupted rows by hand.

explanation.summary: Continuous backup keeps the logs needed to recover to any point in its retention window. Point-in-time recovery creates a new cluster at the chosen timestamp, which you then validate and switch to.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Point-in-time recovery to the moment before the damage.
option_breakdown.B: Read pools serve reads with very little lag and cannot be promoted as a recovery point.
option_breakdown.C: Last night's backup loses a day of good data, and a restore goes into a new cluster anyway.
option_breakdown.D: Hand-editing an export is error-prone and slow.

questions.title: Why a Dataflow job has stopped making progress
questions.summary: The Dataflow job page shows the job graph, per-stage progress, throughput and worker logs.
questions.question: A streaming Dataflow job's output has stopped updating, although the job still shows as running. You need to see which stage is stuck and the errors its workers are logging. Where should you look?

options.A: The Pub/Sub topic's publish rate chart.
options.B: The job's page in the Dataflow monitoring interface.
options.C: The Compute Engine VM list, SSHing into each worker in turn.
options.D: BigQuery's INFORMATION_SCHEMA.JOBS view.

explanation.summary: The Dataflow monitoring interface shows each stage of the job graph with its throughput, data freshness and system lag, plus job and worker logs. A stage with growing lag and errors in its logs is the one that is stuck.

option_breakdown.A: Upstream publish rates show input, not where the pipeline is blocked.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Per-stage status and worker errors in one place.
option_breakdown.C: Workers are managed and short-lived; SSH is slow and misses the job-level view.
option_breakdown.D: INFORMATION_SCHEMA.JOBS lists BigQuery jobs, not Dataflow pipelines.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud dataflow jobs describe JOB_ID --region=REGION
gcloud dataflow jobs list --status=active --region=REGION

questions.title: Checking whether a BigQuery job succeeded
questions.summary: bq show -j (or INFORMATION_SCHEMA.JOBS) reports a BigQuery job's state, errors and bytes processed.
questions.question: A nightly load into BigQuery was started by a script that only recorded the job ID. You need to know whether the job finished, and if not, what error it hit. What should you run?

options.A: `bq ls -j` for last week and assume the newest entry is the job.
options.B: `gcloud logging read` for the dataset name, without a filter.
options.C: `bq show -j JOB_ID`
options.D: `bq head` on the destination table to see whether rows arrived.

explanation.summary: bq show -j prints a job's configuration, state (PENDING, RUNNING, DONE) and any error result. For many jobs, INFORMATION_SCHEMA.JOBS answers the same in SQL.

option_breakdown.A: Listing jobs and guessing is unreliable when you already have the ID.
option_breakdown.B: Unfiltered log searches are slow and noisy compared with asking for the job.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. State and error of that exact job.
option_breakdown.D: Row presence says nothing about failure or partial loads.

questions.title: Fleet-wide database risks across many projects
questions.summary: Database Center gives one view of the database fleet across projects and flags issues like missing backups.
questions.question: Northgate Finance runs about 200 Cloud SQL, AlloyDB and Spanner instances across 60 projects. The security lead wants one place to see which instances lack automated backups, have a public IP address or are not highly available, without building anything. What should you use?

options.A: Query Insights on each instance.
options.B: A Cloud Monitoring dashboard per project.
options.C: The billing export, grouped by SKU.
options.D: Database Center.

explanation.summary: Database Center is the fleet view for Google Cloud databases: an inventory across projects and engines, with health issues such as missing backups, public IP exposure or lack of high availability, and recommendations to fix them.

option_breakdown.A: Query Insights diagnoses query performance on a single instance.
option_breakdown.B: Per-project dashboards show metrics, not configuration risks across the fleet.
option_breakdown.C: Billing rows do not describe backup or network configuration.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. One inventory with the health issues surfaced.

explanation.gcloud_command: # Console > Database Center (filter by issue: no automated backups, public IP, not HA)

questions.title: Database engine versions nearing end of support
questions.summary: Database Center shows engine versions across the fleet, so outdated versions are found in one place.
questions.question: A database team must find every database in the organisation still running an engine version that is approaching end of support, across Cloud SQL, AlloyDB and Spanner, to plan upgrades. What should they use?

options.A: Database Center, filtering the fleet inventory by engine version.
options.B: Query Insights, sorting queries by average latency.
options.C: gcloud sql instances list in each project, copied into a spreadsheet.
options.D: Personalized Service Health.

explanation.summary: Database Center presents the whole database fleet — engine, version, location, project — and surfaces version-related issues, so the upgrade backlog comes from one filtered view.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Fleet-wide inventory including engine versions.
option_breakdown.B: Query Insights is about query performance, not versions.
option_breakdown.C: Per-project loops cover only Cloud SQL and go stale immediately.
option_breakdown.D: Service Health reports Google Cloud incidents, not your databases' versions.

explanation.gcloud_command: # Console > Database Center > filter: Engine version

questions.title: CMEK bucket creation fails on key permission
questions.summary: With CMEK, the service's Google-managed service agent needs Encrypter/Decrypter on the Cloud KMS key.
questions.question: Creating a Cloud Storage bucket with a default customer-managed encryption key fails with a permission error on the key, although you are an Owner of both the project and the key's project. What should you do?

options.A: Grant the Cloud Storage service agent Encrypter/Decrypter on the key.
options.B: Grant yourself Cloud KMS Admin on the key ring.
options.C: Create the key in the same bucket location with the HSM protection level.
options.D: Switch to customer-supplied encryption keys, which need no IAM grant.

explanation.summary: Cloud Storage encrypts and decrypts with the key on your behalf through its service agent (service-PROJECT_NUMBER@gs-project-accounts.iam.gserviceaccount.com). That identity — not you — needs roles/cloudkms.cryptoKeyEncrypterDecrypter on the key.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. The service agent performs the cryptographic operations and needs the role.
option_breakdown.B: Your own permissions are not what the storage service uses.
option_breakdown.C: Protection level does not change who may use the key.
option_breakdown.D: CSEK is a different model with its own drawbacks and does not fix the missing grant.

questions.title: A route to an appliance that drops the traffic
questions.summary: A VM used as a route's next hop must be created with IP forwarding enabled.
questions.question: You add a custom static route sending 172.16.0.0/12 to a firewall appliance VM as its next hop. Packets reach the appliance's interface but are never forwarded onward, although the appliance software is configured correctly. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: The route's priority is 1000, which is too low for custom routes.
options.B: Custom static routes do not support instance next hops.
options.C: The appliance VM doesn't have IP forwarding enabled.
options.D: The subnet needs Private Google Access for routed traffic.

explanation.summary: By default Compute Engine drops packets whose source or destination is not the VM's own address. A VM that forwards traffic — the next hop of a custom route — must be created with IP forwarding enabled.

option_breakdown.A: 1000 is the default priority and is a valid value for custom routes.
option_breakdown.B: Instances are a supported next-hop type for static routes.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Without IP forwarding the VM will not pass through traffic for other addresses.
option_breakdown.D: Private Google Access concerns reaching Google APIs, not routing to an appliance.

questions.title: Finding shadowed and unused firewall rules
questions.summary: Firewall Insights reports shadowed, overly permissive and unused firewall rules from rule-hit data.
questions.question: A VPC has accumulated 400 firewall rules. You want to find the rules that are shadowed by other rules and those with no hits in the last six weeks, so they can be cleaned up safely. What should you use?

options.A: gcloud compute firewall-rules list sorted by priority, reviewed by hand.
options.B: Firewall Insights in Network Intelligence Center.
options.C: VPC Flow Logs exported to BigQuery for a year.
options.D: The IAM role recommender.

explanation.summary: Firewall Insights analyses configuration and firewall-rule hit counts to report shadowed rules, overly permissive rules and rules with no recent hits.

option_breakdown.A: Manual review of 400 rules misses shadowing that depends on overlapping ranges and targets.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Built for this analysis of firewall rules.
option_breakdown.C: Flow logs record connections, not which rule allowed them, and cost more.
option_breakdown.D: The role recommender reduces IAM grants, not firewall rules.

explanation.gcloud_command: # Console > Network Intelligence Center > Firewall Insights

questions.title: Switching a firewall rule off without losing it
questions.summary: A VPC firewall rule can be disabled and re-enabled in place with --disabled / --no-disabled.
questions.question: To test whether a specific allow rule is responsible for some traffic, you want to switch it off for an hour and then restore it exactly as it was. What should you do?

options.A: Delete the rule and recreate it from memory afterwards.
options.B: Change its source range to 0.0.0.0/32 and change it back later.
options.C: Raise its priority number to 65535.
options.D: Disable the rule, then re-enable it.

explanation.summary: A disabled rule stays in the configuration with all its settings but is not enforced; re-enabling it restores the original behaviour exactly.

option_breakdown.A: Recreating from memory risks changing the rule.
option_breakdown.B: Editing ranges is a change to remember and reverse, not a toggle.
option_breakdown.C: An allow rule at 65535 still allows traffic that no other rule decides.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. A clean, reversible toggle.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud compute firewall-rules update allow-web --disabled
gcloud compute firewall-rules update allow-web --no-disabled

questions.title: A business metric emitted by the application
questions.summary: Applications write custom metrics to Cloud Monitoring through OpenTelemetry or the Monitoring API.
questions.question: A Cloud Run service knows how many orders are waiting for fraud review. Operations wants that number charted and alerted on in Cloud Monitoring, sampled every minute. What should you do?

options.A: Log the number at INFO level and read it in the Logs Explorer.
options.B: Estimate it from the service's request count metric.
options.C: Write the value as a custom metric, and alert on it.
options.D: Store the number in a BigQuery table and build a Looker Studio chart.

explanation.summary: Values only the application knows become metrics when the application exports them — through OpenTelemetry with the Google Cloud exporter or directly with the Cloud Monitoring API. They can then be charted and used in alerting policies like any built-in metric.

option_breakdown.A: Reading log lines is not a metric, and alerting would first need a log-based metric.
option_breakdown.B: Request volume does not measure a queue that the application alone tracks.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. An application-emitted metric, alertable like any other.
option_breakdown.D: BigQuery plus a report cannot drive a Cloud Monitoring alerting policy.

explanation.gcloud_command: # OpenTelemetry SDK + Google Cloud Monitoring exporter: gauge 'fraud_review_backlog'

questions.title: Which connections a deny rule blocked
questions.summary: Firewall Rules Logging records the connections a specific rule allowed or denied.
questions.question: An application team says their traffic is being blocked. You suspect one particular deny rule and need a record of the connections it blocks, with source and destination details. What should you enable?

options.A: Data Access audit logs for the Compute Engine API.
options.B: Logging on that firewall rule (Firewall Rules Logging).
options.C: Admin Activity audit logs, which record every packet decision.
options.D: Uptime checks against the application's endpoint.

explanation.summary: Firewall Rules Logging, enabled per rule, writes a log entry for each connection that rule allows or denies, including source, destination, ports and the rule's name.

option_breakdown.A: Data Access logs record API reads, not network traffic.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Per-rule connection records for the suspected rule.
option_breakdown.C: Admin Activity logs record configuration changes, not traffic.
option_breakdown.D: Uptime checks test reachability from outside; they do not say which rule blocked what.

questions.title: Only the errors from one Cloud Run service
questions.summary: The logging query language filters on resource type, labels and severity together.
questions.question: On-call at Pellucid Maps is chasing failures in the Cloud Run service named api. In the Logs Explorer, they want only entries from that service with severity ERROR or worse, and nothing from the project's other Cloud Run services. Which query should they use?

options.A: resource.type="cloud_run_revision" AND textPayload:"api" AND severity=ERROR
options.B: resource.type="cloud_run_revision" AND logName="api" AND severity>=ERROR
options.C: resource.type="cloud_run_revision" AND resource.labels.service_name="api" AND severity>=ERROR
options.D: resource.type="gce_instance" AND resource.labels.service_name="api" AND severity>=ERROR

explanation.summary: Cloud Run entries carry resource.type cloud_run_revision with the service name as a resource label. Severity is ordered, so >= ERROR includes CRITICAL, ALERT and EMERGENCY.

option_breakdown.A: Text matching on "api" catches any message containing the word, and = ERROR misses CRITICAL and worse.
option_breakdown.B: A log name identifies a log, not the Cloud Run service.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Resource, service and severity in the query language.
option_breakdown.D: Cloud Run entries use the cloud_run_revision resource type, not gce_instance.

explanation.gcloud_command: gcloud logging read 'resource.type="cloud_run_revision" AND resource.labels.service_name="api" AND severity>=ERROR' --limit=50

questions.title: Who made a call, and from which address
questions.summary: An audit log entry's protoPayload carries the caller's principal and IP address.
questions.question: You have found the audit log entry for a firewall rule being deleted. You now need the identity that made the call and the IP address it came from. Which fields should you read in the entry?

options.A: protoPayload.serviceName and protoPayload.methodName
options.B: `protoPayload.resourceName` and `protoPayload.request.name`
options.C: `jsonPayload.user` and `httpRequest.remoteIp`
options.D: `protoPayload.authenticationInfo.principalEmail` and `protoPayload.requestMetadata.callerIp`

explanation.summary: Cloud Audit Logs entries use the AuditLog payload. authenticationInfo.principalEmail is the caller, and requestMetadata.callerIp is where the request came from; methodName and resourceName describe what was done.

option_breakdown.A: They say which API method was called, not who called it or from where.
option_breakdown.B: They identify the rule that was deleted, not who deleted it or from where.
option_breakdown.C: Audit entries use protoPayload, not jsonPayload, and httpRequest belongs to request logs.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. The caller identity and source address of the call.

questions.title: Which index would fix the slow queries
questions.summary: Index advisor in Query Insights recommends indexes for slow queries on Cloud SQL and AlloyDB.
questions.question: Query Insights shows that a few queries on a Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL instance account for most of the load, and they scan large tables. You want recommendations for which indexes to create, with the estimated benefit. What should you use?

options.A: Index advisor in Query Insights.
options.B: Cloud Profiler on the database VM.
options.C: The Compute Engine machine-type recommender.
options.D: Cloud Trace for the application calling the database.

explanation.summary: Index advisor analyses the recorded queries and recommends indexes that would speed them up, with the estimated impact and the CREATE INDEX statements to apply.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Index recommendations from the observed query workload.
option_breakdown.B: Cloud SQL is managed; Profiler instruments your own application code.
option_breakdown.C: Machine-type recommendations resize VMs; they do not address missing indexes.
option_breakdown.D: Trace shows that the database call is slow, not which index would help.

explanation.gcloud_command: # Console > Cloud SQL > instance > Query insights > Index advisor

questions.title: Being told when a Google incident affects your projects
questions.summary: Personalized Service Health can alert through Cloud Monitoring on incidents affecting your projects.
questions.question: On-call wants to be notified automatically when Google Cloud posts an incident that affects Cloud SQL in europe-west1 for the projects they run, rather than checking a public status page. What should you configure?

options.A: An uptime check against the public Google Cloud status page.
options.B: A log-based metric on Cloud SQL error logs.
options.C: An alerting policy on Personalized Service Health events.
options.D: A budget alert that fires when Cloud SQL spend changes.

explanation.summary: Personalized Service Health shows Google Cloud incidents relevant to your projects and can drive Cloud Monitoring alerting policies filtered by product, location and relevance.

option_breakdown.A: The public page is not personalised, and polling it is not an integration.
option_breakdown.B: Your own errors may or may not come from a Google incident; this does not report incidents.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Incident notifications scoped to the products and locations you use.
option_breakdown.D: Spend has no relationship to incidents.

explanation.gcloud_command: # Console > Service Health > Configure alerts (product: Cloud SQL, location: europe-west1)

questions.title: One application-centric operations view
questions.summary: Cloud Hub gives an app-centric view of active events, health, deployments and maintenance for App Hub apps.
questions.question: An application team registered their services in App Hub. They want one place, organised by application, that shows active incidents affecting it, upcoming maintenance, recent deployment status and health — rather than switching between product pages. What should they use?

options.A: Cloud Asset Inventory feeds.
options.B: Cloud Hub.
options.C: A Cloud Monitoring metrics scope.
options.D: Query Insights.

explanation.summary: Cloud Hub is an application-centric operations view: for applications registered in App Hub, it brings together active incidents, planned maintenance, deployment status and health in one place.

option_breakdown.A: Asset feeds stream configuration changes; they are not an operations dashboard.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Cloud Hub organises operational events by App Hub application, so the team sees incidents, maintenance, deployments and health for their application together.
option_breakdown.C: A metrics scope aggregates metrics across projects but not incidents, maintenance and deployments by application.
option_breakdown.D: Query Insights is limited to database query performance.

explanation.gcloud_command: # Console > Cloud Hub > select the App Hub application

questions.title: AI-assisted root-cause investigation after an alert
questions.summary: Gemini Cloud Assist investigations correlate logs, metrics and recent changes to suggest likely causes.
questions.question: An alert fired for rising error rates on a GKE workload. The on-call engineer wants an AI-assisted analysis that correlates the relevant logs, metrics and recent configuration changes and proposes likely root causes. What should they start?

options.A: Active Assist's idle VM recommender.
options.B: A new uptime check on the workload.
options.C: Cloud Profiler on every Pod.
options.D: A Gemini Cloud Assist investigation from the alert.

explanation.summary: Gemini Cloud Assist investigations gather signals — logs, metrics, recent changes, known issues — around the affected resources and produce hypotheses about the cause, with next steps.

option_breakdown.A: Idle-resource recommendations are about cost, not incidents.
option_breakdown.B: An uptime check would detect the problem again, not explain it.
option_breakdown.C: Profiler shows CPU hot spots; it does not correlate errors with changes.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. An AI-assisted investigation across logs, metrics and changes.

questions.title: Collecting an application's own log file with the Ops Agent
questions.summary: The Ops Agent reads extra log files when you add a files receiver to its config.yaml and restart it.
questions.question: The Ops Agent is running on a VM and sends system logs, but the application's log file at `/var/log/app/app.log` never appears in Cloud Logging. What should you do?

options.A: A files receiver for that path in the agent's config, then a restart.
options.B: Install the legacy Logging agent alongside the Ops Agent.
options.C: Grant the VM's service account Logs Viewer.
options.D: Move the file to `/var/log/syslog`, the only path the agent can read.

explanation.summary: By default the Ops Agent collects system logs. Other files are added by defining a receiver of type files with their paths, adding it to a pipeline in config.yaml, and restarting the agent.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. A files receiver in the agent's configuration.
option_breakdown.B: Running both agents is unsupported and unnecessary.
option_breakdown.C: Writing logs needs Logs Writer, which the default setup already has; Viewer is for reading.
option_breakdown.D: Any path can be configured; moving application logs is not required.

explanation.gcloud_command: sudo systemctl restart google-cloud-ops-agent   # after adding receivers: app: {type: files, include_paths: [...]}

questions.title: Scraping an application's /metrics endpoint on GKE
questions.summary: With managed collection, a PodMonitoring resource tells Managed Service for Prometheus which Pods to scrape.
questions.question: Managed collection for Google Cloud Managed Service for Prometheus is enabled on Calloway Foods' GKE cluster. A new inventory Deployment exposes Prometheus metrics on port 9090 at /metrics, but after a day none of its metrics appear in Cloud Monitoring. What should you add?

options.A: A PodMonitoring resource for the Pods' metrics port.
options.B: The Ops Agent, installed on every node through a DaemonSet.
options.C: A self-managed Prometheus server with remote write to BigQuery.
options.D: A log-based metric parsing the /metrics output from container logs.

explanation.summary: Managed collection runs the collectors for you, but scraping is opt-in per workload: a PodMonitoring (or ClusterPodMonitoring) resource names the label selector, port and path to scrape.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. It declares what the managed collectors should scrape.
option_breakdown.B: The Ops Agent is for Compute Engine VMs; GKE uses managed collection for Prometheus metrics.
option_breakdown.C: Running your own server is what the managed service replaces, and BigQuery is not a Prometheus backend.
option_breakdown.D: Metrics are scraped over HTTP, not parsed from logs.

explanation.gcloud_command: kubectl apply -f podmonitoring.yaml   # kind: PodMonitoring, selector app=orders, endpoints: port 9090, path /metrics

questions.title: Which Pods are using the most memory right now
questions.summary: kubectl top pods shows live CPU and memory use per Pod from the metrics server.
questions.question: Nodes in a GKE cluster are under memory pressure, and you want to see right now which Pods in namespace shop use the most memory. What should you look at?

options.A: The Pods listed with their status, IPs and nodes.
options.B: A description of the shop namespace's Deployments.
options.C: The cluster's node pools and their machine types.
options.D: Current Pod usage from kubectl top, sorted by memory.

explanation.summary: kubectl top reads current resource usage from the cluster's metrics API and can sort Pods by memory.

option_breakdown.A: get -o wide shows Pod status, IP and node, not resource usage.
option_breakdown.B: describe shows a Deployment's spec, replicas and events, not live consumption.
option_breakdown.C: Listing node pools shows their configuration, not what Pods are using.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. kubectl top reads current resource usage from the cluster's metrics API and can sort Pods by memory.

explanation.gcloud_command:
kubectl top pods -n shop --sort-by=memory
kubectl top nodes

questions.title: Moving a node pool to a bigger machine type
questions.summary: Node machine type is fixed per pool: create a new pool, cordon and drain the old one, then delete it.
questions.question: A GKE Standard node pool of e2-standard-4 nodes must move to n2-standard-8. The team wants to test the new nodes under real load first and be able to move workloads straight back to the old nodes if the new type causes problems. What should you do?

options.A: Create an n2-standard-8 pool, drain the old nodes, and delete the old pool later.
options.B: Update the existing node pool's machine type to n2-standard-8.
options.C: Resize the old pool to zero first, then create the new pool.
options.D: Stop each node VM in Compute Engine and change its machine type.

explanation.summary: A new node pool alongside the old one lets Pods move as old nodes are cordoned and drained, while the old pool still exists to move back to.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Both pools run side by side, so you can drain the old nodes gradually and uncordon them again if the new type misbehaves; delete the old pool only when satisfied.
option_breakdown.B: This is supported, but GKE immediately recreates the pool's nodes with its upgrade strategy, so the old nodes aren't kept to move back to unless you configure a blue-green upgrade.
option_breakdown.C: Scaling the old pool to zero before the new one exists leaves Pods with nowhere to run.
option_breakdown.D: Nodes are managed by the pool's instance group; editing the VMs is unsupported and gets overwritten.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud container node-pools create pool-n2 --cluster=C --location=R --machine-type=n2-standard-8
kubectl cordon NODE && kubectl drain NODE --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data
gcloud container node-pools delete default-pool --cluster=C --location=R

questions.title: HPA and VPA fighting over CPU
questions.summary: Do not let HPA and VPA act on the same CPU or memory metric; scale HPA on another metric or run VPA in recommendation mode.
questions.question: A Deployment has an HPA targeting 60% CPU and a VPA in Auto mode managing CPU requests. Replica counts and Pod sizes oscillate all day. The team wants horizontal scaling plus right-sized requests. What should it change?

options.A: Scale the HPA on another metric, or set the VPA to recommend only.
options.B: Add a second HPA on memory.
options.C: Raise the HPA's maximum replicas.
options.D: Set both HPA and VPA to target 80% CPU.

explanation.summary: When both autoscalers react to CPU, each change triggers the other; separating their signals — or letting VPA only recommend — stops the loop.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. When both autoscalers react to CPU, each change triggers the other; separating their signals — or letting VPA only recommend — stops the loop.
option_breakdown.B: Another HPA adds a third controller to the same fight.
option_breakdown.C: A higher ceiling lets the oscillation grow larger.
option_breakdown.D: Aligning targets keeps both acting on the same metric.

explanation.gcloud_command:
kubectl autoscale deployment web --min=3 --max=30 --cpu-percent=60   # replace with a custom-metric HPA
# VPA spec: updatePolicy: { updateMode: "Off" }   # recommendations only

questions.title: Cheaper Autopilot Pods for interruptible work
questions.summary: Autopilot runs Pods on Spot capacity when they select cloud.google.com/gke-spot: "true".
questions.question: A nightly batch on GKE Autopilot checkpoints its progress and can be interrupted and restarted. The team wants to pay less for it without leaving Autopilot. What should it change in the Pod spec?

options.A: Create a Spot node pool in the cluster.
options.B: Lower the Pods' CPU requests below Autopilot's minimum.
options.C: Add a PriorityClass with a low priority.
options.D: Select Spot Pods with the gke-spot node selector.

explanation.summary: On Autopilot, selecting the gke-spot label asks for Spot Pods, which are billed at Spot prices and may be preempted — acceptable for checkpointed batch.

option_breakdown.A: Autopilot has no node pools for you to create.
option_breakdown.B: Requests below the minimum are raised automatically, so nothing is saved.
option_breakdown.C: Priority affects scheduling order, not the price of capacity.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. On Autopilot, selecting the gke-spot label asks for Spot Pods, which are billed at Spot prices and may be preempted — acceptable for checkpointed batch.

questions.title: Conversation state across turns without building a database
questions.summary: Agent Runtime manages sessions and memory for deployed agents.
questions.question: A support agent built with the Agent Development Kit is deployed to Agent Runtime. Users complain that it forgets what they said two messages earlier. The team does not want to build and run its own conversation store. What should it use?

options.A: Agent Runtime's managed sessions and memory.
options.B: A Memorystore instance written to by the agent code.
options.C: A larger machine type for the agent.
options.D: Cloud Logging, reading earlier prompts back from the logs.

explanation.summary: Agent Runtime provides sessions and memory as managed features, so multi-turn context is kept without the team operating a database.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Agent Runtime provides sessions and memory as managed features, so multi-turn context is kept without the team operating a database.
option_breakdown.B: It would work, but it is a store the team must build, secure and run — what it wants to avoid.
option_breakdown.C: Machine size does not give an agent memory of earlier turns.
option_breakdown.D: Logs are an operational record, not a conversation store, and may hold redacted data.

explanation.gcloud_command:
# Agent Platform SDK: deploy the agent to Agent Runtime, then create a session per conversation
# and pass its session ID with each query

questions.title: A notebook instance with no public IP
questions.summary: Workbench instances can be created without a public IP in a subnet that reaches Google APIs privately.
questions.question: Security requires that Agent Platform Workbench instances used on patient data have no external IP address, yet notebooks must still read from BigQuery and Cloud Storage. What should the administrator do?

options.A: Create the instances with public IPs and a firewall rule denying all ingress.
options.B: Use Cloud Shell for the notebooks instead.
options.C: Give each instance a static external IP allow-listed by BigQuery.
options.D: No public IP, in a subnet with Private Google Access.

explanation.summary: Without a public IP, the instance reaches BigQuery and Cloud Storage through Private Google Access on its subnet, satisfying both requirements.

option_breakdown.A: The instance would still have the external address the policy forbids.
option_breakdown.B: Cloud Shell is not a managed notebook environment for this data.
option_breakdown.C: BigQuery has no IP allow-list, and the requirement forbids external IPs.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Without a public IP, the instance reaches BigQuery and Cloud Storage through Private Google Access on its subnet, satisfying both requirements.

questions.title: Workstations left running overnight
questions.summary: Idle and running timeouts on a workstation configuration stop unused workstations automatically.
questions.question: Developers use Cloud Workstations and often forget to stop them at the end of the day, so the machines run all night. How should the administrator control this for every developer?

options.A: Send a reminder email to developers every evening.
options.B: Delete all workstations every night with a script.
options.C: Idle and running timeouts on the workstation configuration.
options.D: Move developers to smaller machine types.

explanation.summary: Timeouts on the configuration stop any workstation created from it after a period of inactivity (or a maximum running time), with no per-developer action.

option_breakdown.A: Reminders are not a control.
option_breakdown.B: Deleting workstations also discards their persistent home disks.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Timeouts on the configuration stop any workstation created from it after a period of inactivity (or a maximum running time), with no per-developer action.
option_breakdown.D: Smaller machines still cost money all night.

questions.title: Source code to a running service in one command
questions.summary: gcloud run deploy --source builds with Cloud Build, stores the image and deploys it in one step.
questions.question: A developer has a directory with application source and a Dockerfile, no container image yet, and wants the fewest steps to a new Cloud Run revision. What should they run?

options.A: A source deploy, which builds the image and deploys it in one step.
options.B: A local docker build and push, then a deploy of the image.
options.C: A Cloud Build trigger on the repository, then a commit.
options.D: A traffic update that sends everything to the latest revision.

explanation.summary: --source uploads the code, builds it with Cloud Build, stores the image in Artifact Registry and deploys the new revision — one command.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. gcloud run deploy --source uploads the code, builds it with Cloud Build, stores the image in Artifact Registry and deploys the revision, in one command.
option_breakdown.B: That works but is three steps and needs a local Docker daemon.
option_breakdown.C: A trigger is continuous delivery on commits — more set-up, not fewer steps.
option_breakdown.D: update-traffic moves traffic between existing revisions; it builds and deploys nothing.

questions.title: Work that continues after the response is sent
questions.summary: Instance-based billing keeps CPU allocated outside requests, for background work.
questions.question: A Cloud Run service returns 202 immediately and then keeps processing the uploaded file in a background thread. Processing stalls until the next request arrives. What should you change?

options.A: Raise the service's maximum instances.
options.B: Lower the container concurrency to 1.
options.C: Increase the request timeout to 60 minutes.
options.D: Instance-based billing, so CPU stays allocated.

explanation.summary: With request-based billing CPU is throttled outside request handling; instance-based billing keeps CPU allocated so background work can run.

option_breakdown.A: More instances do not give idle instances CPU.
option_breakdown.B: Concurrency controls simultaneous requests per instance, not CPU outside them.
option_breakdown.C: The request already finished; its timeout does not govern background work.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. With request-based billing CPU is throttled outside request handling; instance-based billing keeps CPU allocated so background work can run.

questions.title: GPU drivers for a GKE node pool
questions.summary: GKE can install NVIDIA drivers on a GPU node pool automatically with gpu-driver-version.
questions.question: You add an L4 GPU node pool to a GKE Standard cluster, but Pods that request nvidia.com/gpu fail because the driver is missing. You want GKE to manage the driver. How should the node pool be created?

options.A: The accelerator, plus your own driver-installing DaemonSet.
options.B: Autoscaling on the pool, which installs drivers on scale-up.
options.C: The accelerator with a GKE-managed driver version.
options.D: A Local SSD on each node to hold the driver files.

explanation.summary: Setting gpu-driver-version on the accelerator makes GKE install and manage the NVIDIA driver on the pool's nodes.

option_breakdown.A: A self-managed driver DaemonSet is possible but is exactly what the team wants GKE to do for it.
option_breakdown.B: Autoscaling changes node counts; it installs no drivers.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Setting gpu-driver-version on the accelerator (for example gpu-driver-version=latest) makes GKE install and manage the NVIDIA driver on the pool's nodes.
option_breakdown.D: Storage does not install drivers.

questions.title: Stopping a streaming pipeline without losing data
questions.summary: Draining a Dataflow job finishes in-flight data before stopping; cancelling drops it.
questions.question: Ravensworth Media runs a streaming Dataflow job that reads click events from a Pub/Sub subscription. A new version of the pipeline changes the graph and cannot replace the job in place. No event the running job has already read may be lost. What should you do with the running job?

options.A: Cancel it, then start the new job.
options.B: Update it in place with the new pipeline code.
options.C: Drain it, then start the new job on the same subscription.
options.D: Delete the Pub/Sub subscription to stop input.

explanation.summary: Drain stops reading new input and finishes processing what is in flight before the job stops; unread messages stay in the subscription for the new job.

option_breakdown.A: Cancel stops immediately and loses in-flight data.
option_breakdown.B: An in-place update needs a compatible pipeline graph, which this one is not.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Drain stops reading new input and finishes processing what is in flight before the job stops; unread messages stay in the subscription for the new job.
option_breakdown.D: Deleting the subscription discards its backlog of unacknowledged messages.

questions.title: Which databases would not survive a zone failure
questions.summary: Database Center flags fleet-wide issues such as instances without high availability.
questions.question: An SRE lead must list every Cloud SQL and AlloyDB instance across forty projects that has no high availability configured, and track the list as it changes. What should they use?

options.A: The Cloud SQL instances page, opened in each of the forty projects.
options.B: Query Insights on each instance.
options.C: A spreadsheet maintained by each project owner.
options.D: Database Center, filtered for the missing-HA issue.

explanation.summary: Database Center inventories the database fleet across projects and surfaces availability, security and cost issues, including instances without HA.

option_breakdown.A: Forty per-project views are the fragmentation Database Center removes.
option_breakdown.B: Query Insights diagnoses query performance on one instance.
option_breakdown.C: A hand-kept spreadsheet is out of date the day after it is written.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Database Center inventories the database fleet across projects and surfaces availability, security and cost issues, including instances without HA.

explanation.gcloud_command: # Console > Database Center > Issues > "No high availability"

questions.title: Running a quick query on a Cloud SQL instance
questions.summary: gcloud sql connect opens a client session to a Cloud SQL instance for ad-hoc SQL.
questions.question: From Cloud Shell you need to run a few SELECT statements against the orders database on the Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL instance shop-db. What is the quickest way?

options.A: bq query, naming the Cloud SQL instance.
options.B: An SQL export of shop-db, then read the dump.
options.C: gcloud spanner databases execute-sql on shop-db.
options.D: gcloud sql connect, then SQL at the prompt.

explanation.summary: gcloud sql connect opens the database client (psql here) against the instance, temporarily allowing the connection, so SQL can be run interactively.

option_breakdown.A: bq queries BigQuery, not Cloud SQL (federated queries need a connection set up first).
option_breakdown.B: Exporting a dump is not querying and can take a long time.
option_breakdown.C: execute-sql is a Spanner command.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. gcloud sql connect opens the database client (psql here) against the instance, temporarily allowing the connection, so SQL can be run interactively.

questions.title: Which rule is blocking this connection
questions.summary: Firewall Rules Logging and Connectivity Tests identify the rule that allows or denies a connection.
questions.question: After a change, VM a can no longer reach VM b on TCP 8443 in the same VPC. Dozens of VPC rules and a hierarchical policy apply. You want to know which rule drops the traffic without changing production. What should you run first?

options.A: Delete rules one at a time until the connection works.
options.B: Create an allow-all ingress rule at priority 0 and see whether it helps.
options.C: A Connectivity Test from a to b on TCP 8443.
options.D: Restart VM b.

explanation.summary: Connectivity Tests analyse the configured path — routes, VPC rules and firewall policies — and name the rule or component that drops the packet, without sending production traffic.

option_breakdown.A: Deleting rules in production is dangerous guesswork.
option_breakdown.B: An allow-all rule opens the VM to everything, and still does not tell you which rule was wrong.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Connectivity Tests analyse the configured path — routes, VPC rules and firewall policies — and name the rule or component that drops the packet, without sending production traffic.
option_breakdown.D: A restart does not change firewall evaluation.

questions.title: Adding a partner range to an existing rule
questions.summary: gcloud compute firewall-rules update changes a rule's fields in place; --source-ranges replaces the list.
questions.question: The VPC firewall rule allow-partner-https allows TCP 443 from 198.51.100.0/24. The partner adds 203.0.113.0/24, and both ranges must be allowed. What should you do?

options.A: Update the rule's source ranges to the new range.
options.B: Create a new rule with the same name and the new range.
options.C: Create a route for the new range.
options.D: Update the rule's source ranges to both ranges.

explanation.summary: update replaces the whole source list with the value given, so it must include both the old and the new range.

option_breakdown.A: update replaces the whole source list, so giving only the new range removes the old one.
option_breakdown.B: A rule with that name already exists, so create fails.
option_breakdown.C: Routes decide where outbound traffic goes; they do not allow inbound connections.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. update replaces the source list with the value given, so it must include both the old and the new range.

questions.title: Blocking an attacking address across a whole folder
questions.summary: A deny rule in a hierarchical firewall policy on a folder applies to every VPC beneath it.
questions.question: During an incident, traffic from 192.0.2.66 must be blocked immediately to every VM in the thirty projects of the Retail folder, each with its own VPC. What should you do?

options.A: Add a deny rule to each of the thirty VPCs.
options.B: Add a deny rule to a global network firewall policy in one project.
options.C: A deny rule in a hierarchical policy on the Retail folder.
options.D: Remove the external IP addresses of all VMs in the folder.

explanation.summary: A hierarchical firewall policy on a folder is evaluated before VPC rules in every network beneath it, so one rule blocks the address everywhere at once.

option_breakdown.A: Thirty separate edits are slow during an incident and easy to miss one.
option_breakdown.B: A network firewall policy applies only to the VPCs it is associated with.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. A hierarchical firewall policy on a folder is evaluated before VPC rules in every network beneath it, so one rule blocks the address everywhere at once.
option_breakdown.D: Removing external IPs breaks legitimate service and does not block traffic arriving through load balancers.

questions.title: Cloud VMs resolving on-premises names
questions.summary: A Cloud DNS forwarding zone sends queries for an on-premises domain to on-premises resolvers.
questions.question: Fairhaven Logistics connects a VPC to its data centre over HA VPN. VMs in the VPC must resolve names under corp.internal, which only the on-premises DNS servers at 192.168.10.53 and 192.168.10.54 serve, and records change there daily. What should you configure?

options.A: A private Cloud DNS forwarding zone for corp.internal.
options.B: A public Cloud DNS zone for corp.internal with copies of the records.
options.C: An inbound DNS server policy on the VPC.
options.D: Hard-coded /etc/hosts entries on each VM.

explanation.summary: A forwarding zone makes the VPC's resolver send queries for corp.internal to the on-premises servers over the hybrid connection.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. A forwarding zone makes the VPC's resolver send queries for corp.internal to the on-premises servers over the hybrid connection.
option_breakdown.B: A public zone would publish internal names on the internet and go stale.
option_breakdown.C: An inbound policy is for the opposite direction: on-premises clients resolving Cloud names.
option_breakdown.D: Hosts files are per VM and drift immediately.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud dns managed-zones create corp-fwd --dns-name=corp.internal. --visibility=private \
  --networks=vpc-prod --forwarding-targets=192.168.10.53,192.168.10.54 --description="to on-prem"

questions.title: On-premises servers resolving a Cloud private zone
questions.summary: An inbound server policy gives on-premises resolvers an address in the VPC to forward queries to.
questions.question: Services in a Cloud DNS private zone api.internal.example must be resolvable by on-premises clients connected over Cloud Interconnect. On-premises DNS can forward a domain to any IP address you give it. What should you configure in Google Cloud?

options.A: A forwarding zone for api.internal.example pointing at the on-premises resolvers.
options.B: Make the private zone public so on-premises clients can resolve it.
options.C: A DNS peering zone in the on-premises network.
options.D: An inbound DNS server policy, forwarded to from on-premises DNS.

explanation.summary: An inbound server policy creates resolver entry points in the VPC's subnets that on-premises DNS can forward to, which answer from the private zones visible to the VPC.

option_breakdown.A: A forwarding zone sends queries from Cloud to on-premises — the other direction.
option_breakdown.B: Publishing internal names on the internet is the wrong fix.
option_breakdown.C: Peering zones are between VPC networks in Cloud DNS, not on-premises.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. An inbound server policy creates resolver entry points in the VPC's subnets that on-premises DNS can forward to, which answer from the private zones visible to the VPC.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud dns policies create onprem-inbound --networks=vpc-prod --enable-inbound-forwarding \
  --description="on-prem resolves private zones"

questions.title: A fixed egress address for a partner's allow-list
questions.summary: Cloud NAT with manually assigned static IP addresses gives private VMs a fixed egress address.
questions.question: Payment workers at Olmstead Retail run on VMs without external IPs in a managed instance group that recreates them often. They call a partner's API, and the partner will accept traffic only from two fixed public addresses it adds to an allow-list. What should you configure?

options.A: Give each VM a static external IP address.
options.B: Cloud NAT with two static external IPs, assigned manually.
options.C: Cloud NAT with automatic IP allocation.
options.D: Private Google Access on the subnet.

explanation.summary: Manual NAT IP assignment makes all of the subnet's egress leave from reserved addresses that never change, however often the VMs are recreated.

option_breakdown.A: Static IPs per VM break as the group recreates VMs, and expose the VMs to inbound traffic.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Manual NAT IP assignment makes all of the subnet's egress leave from reserved addresses that never change, however often the VMs are recreated.
option_breakdown.C: Automatic allocation can change or add addresses, which breaks an allow-list.
option_breakdown.D: Private Google Access reaches Google APIs, not a partner's API.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud compute addresses create nat-1 nat-2 --region=REGION
gcloud compute routers nats create nat-cfg --router=nat-router --region=REGION \
  --nat-all-subnet-ip-ranges --nat-external-ip-pool=nat-1,nat-2

questions.title: Keeping the address a VM already has
questions.summary: An ephemeral external IP can be promoted to a static address without changing it.
questions.question: A VM's ephemeral external IP 34.118.10.20 has been given to customers, who allow-list it. The VM must be stopped for maintenance next week, which would release an ephemeral address. What should you do?

options.A: Promote the address in use to a static external IP.
options.B: Reserve a new static external IP and send it to every customer.
options.C: Snapshot the VM so the address is saved with it.
options.D: Set the VM's deletion protection flag.

explanation.summary: Promoting reserves the address the VM already uses, so it survives stop, start and even recreation.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Promoting reserves the address the VM already uses, so it survives stop, start and even recreation.
option_breakdown.B: A new address forces every customer to change their allow-list.
option_breakdown.C: Snapshots capture disk data, not network addresses.
option_breakdown.D: Deletion protection prevents deletion; it does not keep an ephemeral address across a stop.

questions.title: Isolating two subnets by deleting a route
questions.summary: Subnet routes cannot be deleted or overridden by less specific routes; isolate subnets with firewall rules.
questions.question: Security wants VMs in subnet a-sub (10.1.0.0/24) to be unable to open connections to VMs in subnet b-sub (10.2.0.0/24) of the same VPC. An engineer proposes deleting the VPC's route for 10.2.0.0/24. What should you do instead?

options.A: Delete the 10.2.0.0/24 subnet route as proposed.
options.B: Keep the route and add an ingress deny rule on the b-sub VMs for source 10.1.0.0/24.
options.C: Add a custom static route for 10.2.0.0/24 with a lower priority number that points at a blackhole address.
options.D: Move b-sub to a different region.

explanation.summary: Subnet routes are created with each subnet and cannot be deleted, and a custom route cannot override them for the subnet's own range; traffic between subnets is controlled with firewall rules.

option_breakdown.A: Subnet routes cannot be deleted while the subnet exists.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Subnet routes are created with each subnet and cannot be deleted, and a custom route cannot override them for the subnet's own range; traffic between subnets is controlled with firewall rules.
option_breakdown.C: A custom route cannot take precedence over a subnet route for the same destination.
option_breakdown.D: A VPC is global; subnets in different regions still reach each other.

questions.title: Two routes that both match a packet
questions.summary: Route selection prefers the most specific destination prefix before considering priority.
questions.question: A VPC has two custom static routes: 10.0.0.0/8 at priority 100 via appliance A, and 10.5.0.0/16 at priority 900 via appliance B. A VM sends a packet to 10.5.3.4. Which route is used?

options.A: The 10.0.0.0/8 route via appliance A, because its priority number is lower.
options.B: Both, with traffic split equally between them.
options.C: Neither — the default internet route is used.
options.D: The 10.5.0.0/16 route, because the most specific prefix wins.

explanation.summary: Routing first chooses the longest matching prefix; priority breaks ties only among routes with the same destination prefix.

option_breakdown.A: Priority matters only between routes with equally specific destinations.
option_breakdown.B: Equal-cost splitting applies to routes with the same prefix and priority.
option_breakdown.C: The default route 0.0.0.0/0 is the least specific and is used only when nothing else matches.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Routing first chooses the longest matching prefix; priority breaks ties only among routes with the same destination prefix.

questions.title: Latency percentiles from a value in the logs
questions.summary: A distribution log-based metric extracts a numeric field from log entries into a histogram.
questions.question: A legacy service writes a structured log entry per request with jsonPayload.latency_ms, but exports no latency metric. The team wants to chart p50 and p99 latency and alert on p99, without changing code. What should it create?

options.A: A distribution log-based metric on jsonPayload.latency_ms.
options.B: A counter log-based metric on the request entries.
options.C: An uptime check against the service's health endpoint.
options.D: A log sink to BigQuery with a scheduled percentile query.

explanation.summary: A distribution metric turns the extracted values into a histogram time series, from which percentile charts and alert conditions are computed.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. A distribution metric turns the extracted values into a histogram time series, from which percentile charts and alert conditions are computed.
option_breakdown.B: A counter counts entries; it cannot give latency percentiles.
option_breakdown.C: An uptime check measures one probe's response, not the latency of real requests.
option_breakdown.D: A scheduled query is batch analysis, not a metric an alerting policy can evaluate.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud logging metrics create req-latency --config-from-file=latency-metric.yaml
# valueExtractor: EXTRACT(jsonPayload.latency_ms), metricKind DELTA, valueType DISTRIBUTION

questions.title: Prometheus metrics from an application on a VM
questions.summary: The Ops Agent's Prometheus receiver scrapes an application's /metrics endpoint on a VM.
questions.question: A pricing service at Halden Travel runs on Compute Engine VMs and already exposes Prometheus metrics at localhost:9100/metrics. The Ops Agent is installed. The team wants those metrics in Cloud Monitoring without running or maintaining a Prometheus server. What should you add?

options.A: A Prometheus receiver in the Ops Agent configuration
options.B: Rewrite the metrics as log lines and create log-based metrics.
options.C: Deploy a Prometheus server on another VM and point Grafana at it.
options.D: Enable Managed Service for Prometheus managed collection on the project.

explanation.summary: The Ops Agent can scrape Prometheus endpoints on the VM and send the metrics to Cloud Monitoring, where they are queryable with PromQL.
