options.C: Descriptions of the Pods in the default namespace.
options.D: The GKE cluster's own description.

explanation.summary: -A covers all namespaces and the field selector filters on the Pod's phase.

option_breakdown.A: That lists nodes, not Pods.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. kubectl get pods -A --field-selector=status.phase=Pending covers every namespace and filters on the Pod phase.
option_breakdown.C: That covers only one namespace and prints long descriptions.
option_breakdown.D: Cluster configuration does not list Pods.

questions.title: Moving old objects onto the new key version
questions.summary: Rotation does not re-encrypt existing data; rewrite objects so they use the new primary version.
questions.question: A CMEK key protecting a Cloud Storage bucket was rotated after a suspected exposure of the old key version. Security wants every existing object protected by the new primary version, so that the old version can eventually be destroyed. What must happen first?

options.A: Rewrite the existing objects so they use the new version.
options.B: Nothing; rotation already re-encrypted every object with the new version.
options.C: Rotate the key a second time.
options.D: Change the bucket's default key to the same key name.

explanation.summary: Rotation creates a new primary version for new encryption only. Objects written earlier stay encrypted with the older version until they are rewritten.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Rotation creates a new primary version for new encryption only. Objects written earlier stay encrypted with the older version until they are rewritten.
option_breakdown.B: Cloud KMS rotation does not re-encrypt existing data.
option_breakdown.C: Another rotation adds another version and still leaves old objects on the old one.
option_breakdown.D: The default key applies to new writes; it does not touch existing objects.

questions.title: Undoing a key destruction request
questions.summary: Destroyed key versions stay in 'scheduled for destruction' (30 days by default) and can be restored meanwhile.
questions.question: Yesterday an administrator at Cinderford Health scheduled the only enabled version of the Cloud KMS key protecting a production Cloud SQL instance (CMEK) for destruction, by mistake. The key uses the default scheduled-destruction duration. What should you do?

options.A: Restore the key version while it is scheduled for destruction.
options.B: Nothing can be done; destruction is immediate.
options.C: Create a new key with the same name and re-encrypt the database from it.
options.D: Ask Google Cloud support to recover the destroyed key material after the period ends.

explanation.summary: A version scheduled for destruction is kept for the destruction delay (30 days by default). During that time it can be restored; afterwards its material is gone for good.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. A version scheduled for destruction is kept for the destruction delay (30 days by default). During that time it can be restored; afterwards its material is gone for good.
option_breakdown.B: Destruction is delayed precisely so mistakes can be undone.
option_breakdown.C: A new key has different material and cannot decrypt the data.
option_breakdown.D: After destruction, not even Google can recover the key material.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud kms keys versions restore 1 --key=db-key --keyring=data --location=europe-west1
gcloud kms keys versions enable 1 --key=db-key --keyring=data --location=europe-west1

questions.title: Backups that ransomware and rogue admins cannot delete
questions.summary: Backup and DR Service backup vaults enforce a minimum retention that nobody can shorten.
questions.question: After a ransomware incident at a peer company, a CISO requires VM and Cloud SQL backups that nobody, including project owners, can delete or shorten for 30 days after they are taken. What should you use?

options.A: Snapshot schedules with a 30-day retention.
options.B: Backup and DR Service, with a vault enforcing 30-day retention.
options.C: Cloud SQL automated backups with 30 retained backups.
options.D: An IAM condition that denies delete to everyone except owners.

explanation.summary: Backup vaults store backups immutably and indelibly for the enforced retention period, whatever roles the caller holds.

option_breakdown.A: Snapshots can be deleted by anyone with permission.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Backup vaults store backups immutably and indelibly for the enforced retention period, whatever roles the caller holds.
option_breakdown.C: Automated backups disappear if the instance is deleted and can be reconfigured.
option_breakdown.D: Owners could still delete, which is the risk being addressed.

questions.title: Reading Spanner data as it was an hour ago
questions.summary: Spanner point-in-time recovery uses version_retention_period (up to 7 days) for stale reads and restores.
questions.question: A bad batch job overwrote rows in a Spanner database 40 minutes ago. The team wants to read the rows as they were before the job and write them back. The database has version_retention_period set to 1d. What should it do?

options.A: Restore last night's backup over the database.
options.B: Increase version_retention_period now, then read the old values.
options.C: Open a support case to roll back the database.
options.D: A stale read at a time before the job, then write the rows back.

explanation.summary: With a one-day retention, Spanner keeps earlier versions of the data. A read at a past timestamp returns the rows as they were, which can then be written back.

option_breakdown.A: A night-old backup loses everything written since, not just the bad job's changes.
option_breakdown.B: Raising retention now does not bring back versions already expired, and 40 minutes is within the current window anyway.
option_breakdown.C: Recovery is self-service.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. With a one-day retention, Spanner keeps earlier versions of the data. A read at a past timestamp returns the rows as they were, which can then be written back.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud spanner databases execute-sql orders --instance=prod \
  --read-timestamp=2026-09-30T09:00:00Z --sql="SELECT * FROM Accounts WHERE Region='EU'"

questions.title: Joining Cloud SQL rows with BigQuery tables in one query
questions.summary: BigQuery federated queries use EXTERNAL_QUERY through a Cloud SQL connection.
questions.question: An analyst needs today's orders from a Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL database joined with customer segments in BigQuery, without building a pipeline that copies the orders. What should they use?

options.A: A BigQuery external table over the Cloud SQL data directory.
options.B: Query Insights on the Cloud SQL instance.
options.C: A BigQuery connection to Cloud SQL, used with EXTERNAL_QUERY.
options.D: Datastream, then wait for the next daily load.

explanation.summary: Federated queries send a query to Cloud SQL and use its results in BigQuery SQL, so live rows can be joined with warehouse tables.

option_breakdown.A: External tables read files in Cloud Storage, not a database's storage.
option_breakdown.B: Query Insights diagnoses query performance; it does not join data.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Federated queries send a query to Cloud SQL and use its results in BigQuery SQL, so live rows can be joined with warehouse tables.
option_breakdown.D: Replication pipelines are the copying the analyst wants to avoid.

questions.title: Paying for compressed bytes in BigQuery storage
questions.summary: Switching a dataset to the physical storage billing model bills compressed bytes, often far cheaper.
questions.question: A BigQuery dataset at Lowther Telemetry holds 400 TB of logical data that compresses about 8:1, and its tables are rarely updated. Storage is the largest line on the monthly bill, and queries must not change. Which change is most likely to cut storage cost?

options.A: Move the dataset to a multi-region location.
options.B: Switch the dataset to physical-bytes storage billing.
options.C: Turn on table snapshots.
options.D: Set a custom daily query quota.

explanation.summary: Under the physical billing model you pay for compressed bytes (at a higher unit price), which is usually much cheaper for data that compresses well.

option_breakdown.A: Location does not reduce the bytes billed.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Under the physical billing model you pay for compressed bytes (at a higher unit price), which is usually much cheaper for data that compresses well.
option_breakdown.C: Snapshots add storage.
option_breakdown.D: Query quotas limit query spend, not storage.

questions.title: Getting back an object deleted three days ago
questions.summary: Soft delete keeps deleted objects for a retention window (7 days by default), even without versioning.
questions.question: A bucket without Object Versioning has the default soft delete policy. An important object was deleted three days ago. Can it be recovered, and how?

options.A: No: without Object Versioning, a deleted object is gone immediately.
options.B: Yes: restore it from soft delete, which keeps it for 7 days.
options.C: Yes, but only from a machine image of the VM that uploaded it.
options.D: Yes, by asking support to recover it from Google's internal backups.

explanation.summary: Soft delete keeps deleted and overwritten objects for the bucket's retention window, whether or not versioning is enabled, so the object can be restored.

option_breakdown.A: Soft delete works independently of Object Versioning.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Soft delete keeps deleted and overwritten objects for the bucket's retention window, whether or not versioning is enabled, so the object can be restored.
option_breakdown.C: Machine images contain disks, not Cloud Storage objects.
option_breakdown.D: Recovery is self-service within the soft delete window.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud storage ls --soft-deleted gs://reports/q3.pdf
gcloud storage restore gs://reports/q3.pdf#GENERATION

questions.title: Sending only one subnet's traffic through an inspection appliance
questions.summary: A policy-based route matches source/destination/protocol and sends matching traffic to an internal LB.
questions.question: Traffic from the subnet 10.20.0.0/24 to the internet must pass through a group of firewall appliance VMs behind an internal passthrough Network Load Balancer. Traffic from all other subnets must keep its normal path. What should you create?

options.A: A static route 0.0.0.0/0 with the appliance as next hop and a higher priority.
options.B: A Cloud NAT gateway for 10.20.0.0/24.
options.C: A firewall rule that denies egress from 10.20.0.0/24.
options.D: A policy-based route on source 10.20.0.0/24, to the load balancer.

explanation.summary: Policy-based routes can match on the source range, which destination-based static routes cannot, and forward matching traffic to an internal passthrough load balancer.

option_breakdown.A: A default route applies to every subnet (or tagged VMs), not by source subnet.
option_breakdown.B: NAT translates addresses; it does not insert an appliance.
option_breakdown.C: Denying traffic is not routing it through inspection.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Policy-based routes can match on the source range, which destination-based static routes cannot, and forward matching traffic to an internal passthrough load balancer.

questions.title: A highly available next hop for a static route
questions.summary: Use an internal passthrough Network Load Balancer as next hop to spread across healthy appliances.
questions.question: A custom static route sends traffic for 172.16.0.0/12 to a single appliance VM. When that VM fails, traffic is dropped. You now run two appliance VMs. How should the route change?

options.A: Create two routes with the same priority, one per appliance VM.
options.B: Put the appliances behind an internal passthrough NLB as next hop.
options.C: Use --next-hop-gateway=default-internet-gateway.
options.D: Add a second network interface to the failed VM.

explanation.summary: With an internal passthrough load balancer as the next hop, traffic goes only to backends that pass health checks, so a failed appliance is taken out automatically.

option_breakdown.A: Equal-priority routes to instances spread traffic but keep sending to a failed VM while it still exists.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. With an internal passthrough load balancer as the next hop, traffic goes only to backends that pass health checks, so a failed appliance is taken out automatically.
option_breakdown.C: The internet gateway bypasses the appliances.
option_breakdown.D: Extra interfaces do not make a failed VM healthy.

questions.title: A peered VPC that cannot see the VPN routes
questions.summary: Export custom routes on one side and import them on the other for peered VPCs to use them.
questions.question: VPC hub has an HA VPN to on-premises with dynamic routes. VPC app is peered with hub, but VMs in app cannot reach on-premises. Subnet routes work fine across the peering. What should you configure?

options.A: Create a second HA VPN from app to on-premises.
options.B: Add a static route in app pointing at the VPN tunnel in hub.
options.C: Enable Private Google Access on app's subnets.
options.D: Export custom routes on hub's peering and import them on app's.

explanation.summary: Peering exchanges subnet routes by default. Custom routes, including dynamic routes learned over VPN, are shared only when exported by one side and imported by the other. On-premises must also learn app's ranges.

option_breakdown.A: A second VPN works but is unnecessary duplication.
option_breakdown.B: A route cannot point at a tunnel in another VPC.
option_breakdown.C: Private Google Access is for reaching Google APIs.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Peering exchanges subnet routes by default. Custom routes, including dynamic routes learned over VPN, are shared only when exported by one side and imported by the other. On-premises must also learn app's ranges.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud compute networks peerings update hub-to-app --network=hub --export-custom-routes
gcloud compute networks peerings update app-to-hub --network=app --import-custom-routes

questions.title: A GKE cluster that has run out of Pod addresses
questions.summary: Add an additional (discontiguous) Pod IPv4 range and use it for new node pools.
questions.question: A VPC-native GKE cluster cannot add nodes because its Pod secondary range is exhausted, and the range cannot be expanded because neighbouring ranges are in use. What should you do?

options.A: Recreate the cluster with a larger Pod range.
options.B: Switch the cluster to routes-based networking.
options.C: Lower the maximum Pods per node on the existing node pool in place.
options.D: Add a secondary range for Pods, used by new node pools.

explanation.summary: GKE supports additional, discontiguous Pod ranges. New node pools can take their Pod IPs from a new secondary range, so the cluster keeps growing without being recreated.

option_breakdown.A: Recreating the cluster is disruptive and unnecessary.
option_breakdown.B: A cluster cannot be converted from VPC-native to routes-based.
option_breakdown.C: Max Pods per node cannot be changed on an existing node pool.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. GKE supports additional, discontiguous Pod ranges. New node pools can take their Pod IPs from a new secondary range, so the cluster keeps growing without being recreated.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud compute networks subnets update gke-subnet --region=us-central1 \
  --add-secondary-ranges=pods-2=10.64.0.0/14
gcloud container node-pools create pool-2 --cluster=prod --location=us-central1 --pod-ipv4-range=pods-2

questions.title: One address for a global load balancer that must never change
questions.summary: Reserve a global static external IP address and use it in the global forwarding rule.
questions.question: Customers allow-list the IP address of your global external Application Load Balancer, which you will rebuild next month. The address must stay the same. What should you do?

options.A: Reserve a regional static external IP address in us-central1.
options.B: Keep the ephemeral address by never deleting the forwarding rule.
options.C: Reserve a global static external IP for the new forwarding rule.
options.D: Use the load balancer's DNS name instead of an IP.

explanation.summary: Global load balancers need global addresses. A reserved static address stays in the project and can be attached to a new forwarding rule.

option_breakdown.A: A regional address cannot be used by a global forwarding rule.
option_breakdown.B: The rebuild will delete the forwarding rule, releasing an ephemeral address.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Global load balancers need global addresses. A reserved static address stays in the project and can be attached to a new forwarding rule.
option_breakdown.D: The customers allow-list an IP address, not a DNS name.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud compute addresses create shop-ip --global --ip-version=IPV4
gcloud compute forwarding-rules create shop-fr --global --address=shop-ip --target-https-proxy=shop-proxy --ports=443

questions.title: Every firewall rule that actually applies to one VM
questions.summary: get-effective-firewalls shows hierarchical, network-policy and VPC rules applying to an interface.
questions.question: A VM is subject to organisation and folder firewall policies, a global network firewall policy and VPC firewall rules. You need the combined list of rules that apply to its network interface. What should you look at?

options.A: The effective firewalls of the VM's network interface.
options.B: The VPC network's list of firewall rules.
options.C: The organisation's hierarchical firewall policies.
options.D: The VM's own instance description.

explanation.summary: The effective firewalls view combines every policy and rule that applies to the interface, from the organisation down.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. gcloud compute instances network-interfaces get-effective-firewalls combines every policy and rule that applies to the interface, from the organisation down.
option_breakdown.B: That lists VPC firewall rules only, not policies.
option_breakdown.C: That lists hierarchical policies, not what applies to the VM.
option_breakdown.D: Instance details do not include firewall rules.

explanation.gcloud_command: gcloud compute instances network-interfaces get-effective-firewalls app-1 --zone=us-central1-a

questions.title: NAT port exhaustion on a few busy VMs
questions.summary: Dynamic port allocation lets busy VMs get more NAT ports while quiet VMs keep few.
questions.question: A handful of VMs behind Cloud NAT open thousands of connections to the same API and see dropped connections, and NAT logs show OUT_OF_RESOURCES. Most other VMs use few connections. What should you change, without reserving more ports for the idle VMs?

options.A: Raise the static minimum ports per VM for every VM.
options.B: Remove Cloud NAT and give the busy VMs external IPs.
options.C: Dynamic port allocation on the NAT gateway.
options.D: Enable Private Google Access.

explanation.summary: Dynamic port allocation starts each VM with a minimum and grows its allocation on demand up to a maximum, so busy VMs get more ports without reserving them for everyone.

option_breakdown.A: A higher static minimum wastes NAT addresses on idle VMs.
option_breakdown.B: External IPs remove the egress controls NAT provides.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Dynamic port allocation starts each VM at a minimum and grows its allocation on demand up to a maximum, so busy VMs get more ports without reserving them for everyone.
option_breakdown.D: Private Google Access is only for Google APIs.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud compute routers nats update prod-nat --router=prod-router --region=us-central1 \
  --enable-dynamic-port-allocation --min-ports-per-vm=64 --max-ports-per-vm=8192

questions.title: A cryptic log entry during an incident
questions.summary: Logs Explorer can ask Gemini Cloud Assist to explain a log entry in plain language.
questions.question: During an incident, an on-call engineer finds an unfamiliar error entry from a GKE system component in Logs Explorer and does not know what it means. With Gemini Cloud Assist set up, what is the quickest help?

options.A: Create a log-based metric for the entry.
options.B: Use Explain this log entry on the entry in Logs Explorer.
options.C: Route the entry to BigQuery and query it.
options.D: Increase the log bucket's retention.

explanation.summary: Gemini Cloud Assist can summarise what a log entry means and suggest next steps, right from Logs Explorer.

option_breakdown.A: A metric counts entries; it does not explain them.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Gemini Cloud Assist can summarise what a log entry means and suggest next steps, right from Logs Explorer.
option_breakdown.C: Querying in BigQuery does not explain the message.
option_breakdown.D: Retention has nothing to do with understanding the entry.

explanation.gcloud_command: # Logs Explorer > expand the entry > Explain this log entry

questions.title: Which application's deployment failed last night
questions.summary: Cloud Hub's deployments view shows recent GKE and Cloud Run deployments, including failed App Hub ones.
questions.question: Your applications are defined in App Hub. A manager asks each morning which applications had failed deployments overnight on GKE or Cloud Run. Where can you see this in one place?

options.A: Personalized Service Health.
options.B: Active Assist recommendations.
options.C: Cloud Asset Inventory history.
options.D: The Deployments page of Cloud Hub.

explanation.summary: Cloud Hub's deployments view lists recent application deployments to GKE and Cloud Run and highlights failed App Hub application deployments.

option_breakdown.A: Service Health covers Google-side incidents, not your deployments.
option_breakdown.B: Recommendations are about optimisation.
option_breakdown.C: Asset history shows configuration changes, not deployment outcomes per application.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Cloud Hub's deployments view lists recent application deployments to GKE and Cloud Run and highlights failed App Hub application deployments.

questions.title: Cost of one application across its projects
questions.summary: Cloud Hub's Optimization page shows cost and utilisation per project or App Hub application.
questions.question: The checkout application, defined in App Hub, uses resources in three projects. A product owner wants its total cost trend and its most expensive workloads without writing billing queries. Where should they look?

options.A: The billing account's payment history.
options.B: Cloud Hub's Optimization view, for checkout.
options.C: Database Center.
options.D: The Personalized Service Health dashboard.

explanation.summary: Cloud Hub summarises cost and utilisation for a project or an App Hub application, including its trend and its top workloads by cost.

option_breakdown.A: Payments are invoices, not per-application cost.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Cloud Hub summarises cost and utilisation for a project or an App Hub application, including its trend and its top workloads by cost.
option_breakdown.C: Database Center covers databases only.
option_breakdown.D: Service Health shows Google incidents.

explanation.gcloud_command: # Console > Cloud Hub > Optimization > Application: checkout

questions.title: Paging on how fast the error budget is burning
questions.summary: An SLO burn-rate alert pages when the error budget is being consumed too quickly.
questions.question: A service has a 99.9% availability SLO over 28 days in Cloud Monitoring. The team wants to be paged when errors are consuming the error budget fast enough to exhaust it long before the period ends, not on every small blip. What alert should it create?

options.A: A burn-rate alerting policy on the SLO.
options.B: A threshold alert on any HTTP 5xx.
options.C: An uptime check from three regions.
options.D: A log-based alert on every error entry.

explanation.summary: Burn-rate alerts compare the current rate of budget consumption with the rate that would exactly use it up, which ignores small blips but catches serious trends.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Burn-rate alerts compare the current rate of budget consumption with the rate that would exactly use it up, which ignores small blips but catches serious trends.
option_breakdown.B: Any 5xx pages on blips, the noise to avoid.
option_breakdown.C: Uptime checks test reachability, not budget consumption.
option_breakdown.D: Per-error alerts are even noisier.

explanation.gcloud_command: # Monitoring > Services > checkout > SLO > Create SLO alert: burn rate 10 over a 1-hour lookback

questions.title: Testing a multi-step checkout journey every five minutes
questions.summary: Synthetic monitors run scripted tests (such as browser flows) on a schedule and alert on failure.
questions.question: An uptime check confirms the shop's home page returns 200, but last week the checkout flow broke while the home page stayed up. The team wants a scripted test that logs in, adds an item and checks out every five minutes. What should it use?

options.A: A synthetic monitor running a scripted browser test.
options.B: An uptime check on the checkout URL.
options.C: A log-based metric on checkout errors.
options.D: Cloud Trace sampling at 100%.

explanation.summary: Synthetic monitors run your test code on a schedule, including multi-step browser flows, and report results and failures to Cloud Monitoring for alerting.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Synthetic monitors run your test code on a schedule, including multi-step browser flows, and report results and failures to Cloud Monitoring for alerting.
option_breakdown.B: An uptime check requests one URL; it cannot log in and complete a flow.
option_breakdown.C: A log metric depends on real users hitting the failure first.
option_breakdown.D: Tracing shows latency of real requests; it does not test flows.

explanation.gcloud_command: # Monitoring > Synthetic monitoring > Create synthetic monitor > Mocha/Puppeteer template, every 5 min

questions.title: An uptime check for a service with no public address
questions.summary: Private uptime checks reach internal endpoints through Service Directory.
questions.question: An internal HR API runs behind an internal load balancer with no external IP. The team wants an uptime check and alert on it like its public services. What should it configure?

options.A: A public uptime check against the internal IP address.
options.B: A private uptime check through a Service Directory endpoint.
options.C: An external IP on the load balancer for the uptime checkers only.
options.D: A VM running curl in a cron job.

explanation.summary: Private uptime checks reach internal resources through Service Directory, with firewall rules for the checkers' ranges, so the API stays internal.

option_breakdown.A: Public checkers cannot reach private IP addresses.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Private uptime checks reach internal resources through Service Directory, with firewall rules for the checkers' ranges, so the API stays internal.
option_breakdown.C: Exposing the API defeats its internal design.
option_breakdown.D: A self-built checker is extra infrastructure without uptime-check reporting.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud service-directory services create hr-api --namespace=internal --location=us-central1
# Monitoring > Uptime checks > Create > Internal IP (Service Directory service hr-api)

questions.title: Existing Grafana dashboards on Managed Service for Prometheus
questions.summary: Grafana queries Managed Service for Prometheus with PromQL through a Cloud Monitoring data source.
questions.question: A team moved from self-managed Prometheus to Google Cloud Managed Service for Prometheus but wants to keep its Grafana dashboards, which use PromQL. What should it do?

options.A: Rewrite every dashboard in MQL.
options.B: Keep running the old Prometheus servers only for Grafana.
options.C: Export metrics to BigQuery and query them from Grafana with SQL.
options.D: Point Grafana at the service's Prometheus-compatible API.

explanation.summary: Managed Service for Prometheus supports PromQL through a Prometheus-compatible API, so Grafana dashboards keep working with a data source change.

option_breakdown.A: No rewrite is needed; PromQL is supported.
option_breakdown.B: Running old servers defeats the move.
option_breakdown.C: SQL rewrites are unnecessary.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Managed Service for Prometheus supports PromQL through a Prometheus-compatible API, so Grafana dashboards keep working with a data source change.

explanation.gcloud_command:
# Deploy the data source syncer so Grafana's Prometheus data source authenticates to
# https://monitoring.googleapis.com/v1/projects/P/location/global/prometheus

questions.title: OpenTelemetry-instrumented services on Google Cloud
questions.summary: Send OpenTelemetry metrics and traces to Cloud Monitoring and Cloud Trace through an OpenTelemetry Collector.
questions.question: A team instruments its services with OpenTelemetry SDKs so it is not tied to one vendor. It wants the metrics in Cloud Monitoring and the traces in Cloud Trace, without changing the instrumentation. What should it deploy?

options.A: The Ops Agent's legacy Monitoring agent configuration only.
options.B: Rewrite the instrumentation with the Cloud Monitoring client library.
options.C: An OpenTelemetry Collector that exports to Google Cloud.
options.D: Log-based metrics on the application's stdout.

explanation.summary: An OpenTelemetry Collector receives OTLP from the SDKs and exports metrics and traces to Cloud Monitoring and Cloud Trace, so the code stays vendor-neutral.

option_breakdown.A: That collects VM system metrics, not the application's OTLP telemetry.
option_breakdown.B: Rewriting ties the code to one vendor, which the team wants to avoid.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. An OpenTelemetry Collector receives OTLP from the SDKs and exports metrics and traces to Cloud Monitoring and Cloud Trace, so the code stays vendor-neutral.
option_breakdown.D: Log parsing loses the structured metrics and traces.

explanation.gcloud_command: # collector config: receivers: otlp; exporters: googlecloud (traces), googlemanagedprometheus (metrics)

questions.title: VPC Flow Logs costing more than they are worth
questions.summary: Lower the sampling rate and lengthen the aggregation interval to reduce flow log volume.
questions.question: VPC Flow Logs on a busy subnet are used for weekly traffic analysis, but their volume has become a large part of the logging bill. Exact per-connection records are not needed. What should you change?

options.A: Lower the sampling rate and lengthen the aggregation interval.
options.B: Disable flow logs and rely on firewall rules logging.
options.C: Route flow logs to a bucket with 1-day retention.
options.D: Enable Data Access audit logs instead.

explanation.summary: Sampling and aggregation settings control how many flow records are generated, which cuts volume and cost while keeping the traffic picture.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Sampling and aggregation settings control how many flow records are generated, which cuts volume and cost while keeping the traffic picture.
option_breakdown.B: Firewall logs cover only traffic matched by logged rules.
option_breakdown.C: Shorter retention still pays to ingest every record.
option_breakdown.D: Audit logs record API calls, not network flows.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud compute networks subnets update web --region=us-central1 \
  --logging-flow-sampling=0.1 --logging-aggregation-interval=interval-5-min

questions.title: What TERMINATED means in the instance list
questions.summary: TERMINATED means stopped, not deleted: the VM still exists and its disks and reserved addresses still cost money.
questions.question: While checking what is running in a project, you see a VM reported with the status TERMINATED in the output of gcloud compute instances list. A teammate assumes the VM has been deleted and that nothing about it is still billed. What is actually true?

options.A: The VM was deleted, and it stays in the list for 30 days before it disappears.
options.B: The VM is stopped. It can be started again, and its persistent disks are still billed.
options.C: The VM crashed and Compute Engine will restart it automatically within the hour.
options.D: The VM is suspended, and its memory contents are preserved and billed until it resumes.

explanation.summary: In Compute Engine, TERMINATED is the state of a stopped VM. A deleted VM is not listed at all. You stop paying for vCPUs and memory, but attached disks and static IP addresses continue to be charged.

option_breakdown.A: A deleted instance no longer appears in the list; there is no 30-day listing period.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. TERMINATED is the stopped state: the instance resource remains, it can be started, and its disks keep costing money.
option_breakdown.C: Stopping does not schedule a restart, and TERMINATED does not by itself mean a crash. Automatic restart applies when a VM configured for it crashes or Compute Engine stops it for a programmed stop, such as a maintenance event.
option_breakdown.D: A suspended VM is reported as SUSPENDED, a different state from TERMINATED.

questions.title: Every VM in the organization, not one project
questions.summary: gcloud compute instances list is scoped to one project; Cloud Asset Inventory searches across an organization.
questions.question: A security review needs a single list of every Compute Engine instance across all of the several hundred projects in your organization. You want to avoid writing a script that loops over projects. What should you use?

options.A: The Compute Engine instance list, run against the organisation.
options.B: The console's VM instances page, filtered on the organisation.
options.C: Cloud Asset Inventory search, scoped to the organisation and instances.
options.D: A billing export to BigQuery, grouped by project.

explanation.summary: Cloud Asset Inventory searches resources across a project, folder or organization scope, so with the search permission granted on the organization, one command covers every project under it.

option_breakdown.A: gcloud compute instances list works on one project at a time; it has no organisation scope.
option_breakdown.B: The VM instances page shows the instances of the selected project.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. gcloud asset search-all-resources --scope=organizations/ORG_ID --asset-types=compute.googleapis.com/Instance lists them all in one call.
option_breakdown.D: Billing data records charges and SKUs, not an inventory of the instances that currently exist.

questions.title: Applying a lifecycle configuration from a file
questions.summary: A lifecycle configuration is a bucket-level JSON document, applied with gcloud storage buckets update --lifecycle-file.
questions.question: You wrote a JSON file containing the lifecycle rules for an existing bucket that stores build artifacts. You want the rules to take effect on the bucket from now on. What should you do?

options.A: Update every object in the bucket with the lifecycle file.
options.B: Update the bucket's lifecycle configuration from the file.
options.C: Copy the file into the bucket under a special name.
options.D: Create the bucket again, passing the file.

explanation.summary: Lifecycle configuration belongs to the bucket, not to individual objects, so it is set by updating the bucket with the JSON file.

option_breakdown.A: Lifecycle rules are not an object property, so an object-level update cannot set them.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. gcloud storage buckets update gs://build-artifacts --lifecycle-file=rules.json sets the bucket's lifecycle configuration.
option_breakdown.C: Copying a file into a bucket only stores it as an object; no special file name configures the bucket.
option_breakdown.D: The bucket already exists, and create would fail rather than change its configuration.

questions.title: A live-only age rule that never frees versioned storage
questions.summary: With Object Versioning on, a Delete rule limited to isLive true only makes live objects noncurrent; removing those versions needs a rule that can match them.
questions.question: A bucket has Object Versioning enabled and one lifecycle rule: Delete when age is 365 days and isLive is true. A year later the rule is clearly firing, because old objects no longer show in a normal listing, yet the bucket's stored bytes keep growing. What should you change?

options.A: Move the bucket to the Archive class, because lifecycle deletions do not apply to Standard objects.
options.B: Disable Object Versioning, which permanently removes all existing noncurrent versions.
options.C: Replace the lifecycle rule with a nightly script that deletes the old objects by name.
options.D: Add a rule that deletes noncurrent versions, for example with a daysSinceNoncurrentTime condition.

explanation.summary: On a versioned bucket, a Delete action applied to a live object turns it into a noncurrent version, which keeps being stored and billed. This rule requires isLive to be true, so it never matches those versions. Without that condition, an age rule would also delete noncurrent versions past that age on a later run.

option_breakdown.A: Lifecycle actions apply in every storage class, and Archive would add retrieval costs without removing anything.
option_breakdown.B: Disabling versioning stops new versions being kept but leaves existing noncurrent versions in place.
option_breakdown.C: A script deleting live objects has the same effect as the rule and leaves the same noncurrent versions behind.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. daysSinceNoncurrentTime is satisfied once a version has been noncurrent for the set number of days, so the rule removes the versions consuming the storage. numNewerVersions alone would not clear them all, because the newest noncurrent version of an object with no live version has no newer versions.

questions.title: Deleting Coldline objects after a month
questions.summary: Each colder class has a minimum storage duration; deleting early is charged as if the object stayed the full minimum.
questions.question: To lower storage cost, a team stores temporary exports in Coldline Storage and deletes each export 30 days after writing it. The exports are almost never read. When you review the estimate, what should you point out?

options.A: Coldline bills only for the 30 days stored, so the estimate only needs to compare the per-GB rates.
options.B: Objects deleted before the Coldline minimum are rejected, so the 30-day deletion will fail.
options.C: Each export is billed for Coldline's 90-day minimum; Nearline may cost less.
options.D: Coldline has no minimum duration, but each deletion costs the same as retrieving the whole object.

explanation.summary: Nearline, Coldline and Archive have minimum storage durations of 30, 90 and 365 days. Early deletion is allowed, and it is charged as though the object had been stored for the full minimum.

option_breakdown.A: This ignores the minimum duration, which is what makes short-lived data expensive in a cold class.
option_breakdown.B: Early deletion succeeds; the consequence is a charge, not an error.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Thirty days in Coldline is billed as 90, so a warmer class such as Nearline, whose minimum is only 30 days, can cost less for this pattern. Compare the rates for your location.
option_breakdown.D: Coldline does have a minimum duration, and the charge is for the remaining storage time rather than a retrieval.

explanation.gcloud_command: # Pricing Calculator > Cloud Storage: compare Coldline and Nearline for objects kept 30 days

questions.title: New revisions that never receive traffic
questions.summary: Once traffic is pinned to a named revision, new deployments get no traffic until it is sent to the latest revision again.
questions.question: Months ago, an engineer sent 100% of a Cloud Run service's traffic to revision api-00041 during an incident. Since then, every deployment succeeds, but users still reach api-00041 and the new revisions serve nothing. What should you do?

options.A: Send traffic to the latest revision, so future deployments receive it automatically.
options.B: Delete revision api-00041 so that Cloud Run is forced to move traffic.
options.C: Raise the service's minimum instances so the new revisions start.
options.D: Redeploy the same image with a new tag on every release.

explanation.summary: Pinning traffic to a specific revision stops new revisions from receiving it. Routing traffic to the latest revision again makes each new deployment serve traffic.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. update-traffic --to-latest sends traffic to the newest ready revision, and future deployments follow automatically.
option_breakdown.B: A revision that is serving traffic can't be deleted, and deleting revisions isn't how traffic is routed.
option_breakdown.C: Minimum instances keep instances warm; they don't route traffic to a revision.
option_breakdown.D: A tag gives a revision its own URL; it sends it no production traffic.

questions.title: Changing an environment variable on Cloud Run
questions.summary: Any configuration change to a Cloud Run service, such as an environment variable, creates a new revision.
questions.question: You change the LOG_LEVEL environment variable of a running Cloud Run service from info to debug, without changing its container image. Traffic is set to follow the latest revision. What happens?

options.A: Running instances pick up the new value within a minute, with no new revision.
options.B: Nothing happens until the image is rebuilt and pushed again.
options.C: The change is saved and applies the next time the service scales from zero.
options.D: A new revision is created with the new value, and it receives the traffic.

explanation.summary: Revisions are immutable. Changing configuration such as an environment variable deploys a new revision, and with traffic following the latest revision, it serves the requests.

option_breakdown.A: Revisions are immutable, so running instances keep the configuration they started with.
option_breakdown.B: Configuration changes don't need a new image; the existing image is reused.
option_breakdown.C: There is no deferred configuration; the change takes effect as a new revision immediately.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. The service gets a new revision with LOG_LEVEL=debug, and traffic moves to it.

questions.title: Clearing out abandoned multipart uploads
questions.summary: The AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload lifecycle action removes multipart uploads left unfinished for a set number of days.
questions.question: A backup tool uploads large files to a bucket through the XML API's multipart uploads. When it crashes, it leaves unfinished uploads whose parts are still stored and billed. You want those cleaned up automatically after seven days. What should you configure?

options.A: A Delete rule for objects older than seven days.
options.B: An AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload rule with an age of seven days.
options.C: A soft delete policy with a seven-day retention.
options.D: Object Versioning, with a rule for noncurrent versions.

explanation.summary: Parts of an unfinished multipart upload aren't objects yet, so object rules don't touch them. The AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload lifecycle action removes uploads left incomplete for the given age.

option_breakdown.A: A Delete rule acts on objects, and it would also delete the completed backups.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. The action aborts multipart uploads that stay incomplete for seven days, which deletes their parts.
option_breakdown.C: Soft delete keeps deleted objects for recovery; it doesn't remove unfinished uploads.
option_breakdown.D: Versioning keeps older generations of objects; unfinished uploads aren't versions.

questions.title: A lifecycle rule that has not acted yet
questions.summary: Lifecycle actions are asynchronous; after you add or change a rule, it can take up to 24 hours to take effect.
questions.question: An hour ago you added a lifecycle rule that deletes objects older than 30 days. Objects that are 200 days old are still listed in the bucket. The rule's JSON is correct. What is the most likely explanation?

options.A: Lifecycle rules apply only to objects created after the rule was added.
options.B: The bucket must be in the Nearline class for Delete actions to run.
options.C: Objects must carry a label naming the rule before it acts on them.
options.D: Lifecycle changes can take up to 24 hours to take effect, and actions run asynchronously.

explanation.summary: Cloud Storage evaluates lifecycle rules asynchronously. A new or changed configuration can take up to 24 hours to take effect, and objects are then acted on in the background.

option_breakdown.A: Rules apply to existing objects that meet the condition, not only new ones.
option_breakdown.B: Delete actions work in every storage class.
option_breakdown.C: Rules match on conditions such as age; no label is needed.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. The rule is fine; Cloud Storage hasn't applied it yet.

questions.title: Pausing a VM with its memory kept
questions.summary: Suspending a VM saves its memory to storage and lets it resume where it left off; stopping discards memory.
questions.question: A developer's VM runs a long interactive analysis that takes an hour to load into memory. Each evening they want to pause it so vCPUs aren't billed overnight, then continue next morning without reloading. What should they do each evening?

options.A: Stop the VM and start it again in the morning.
options.B: Delete the VM and recreate it from a machine image.
options.C: Suspend the VM and resume it in the morning.
options.D: Resize the VM to an e2-micro machine type overnight.

explanation.summary: Suspend preserves the guest's memory and device state, so the VM resumes where it left off. While suspended you pay for the preserved memory and the disks, not for vCPUs.

option_breakdown.A: Stopping shuts the guest down, so memory is lost and the analysis must reload.
option_breakdown.B: A machine image captures disks and configuration, not running memory.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Suspend saves memory to storage, and resume restores the running state.
option_breakdown.D: Changing the machine type needs a stop, which loses memory too.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud compute instances suspend analysis-1 --zone=ZONE
gcloud compute instances resume analysis-1 --zone=ZONE

questions.title: Giving a running VM more vCPUs
questions.summary: A VM's machine type can be changed only while it is stopped.
questions.question: A standalone n2-standard-4 VM needs to become n2-standard-8, keeping its boot disk, internal IP address and metadata. What is the procedure?

options.A: Stop the VM, change its machine type, then start it.
options.B: Change the machine type while it runs; vCPUs are hot-added.
options.C: Create a snapshot and build a new VM of the larger type from it.
options.D: Attach a second n2-standard-4 to the VM as an accelerator.

explanation.summary: Compute Engine changes a VM's machine type only when the VM is stopped. The disks, addresses and metadata stay with the instance.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Stop, set the new machine type, and start; the instance keeps its disks and configuration.
option_breakdown.B: vCPUs and memory can't be hot-added; the VM must be stopped.
option_breakdown.C: A new VM works, but it is a different instance with new settings to recreate, which is more work than needed.
option_breakdown.D: Machine types aren't accelerators and can't be attached to a VM.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud compute instances stop app-1 --zone=ZONE
gcloud compute instances set-machine-type app-1 --zone=ZONE --machine-type=n2-standard-8
gcloud compute instances start app-1 --zone=ZONE

questions.title: A BigQuery job that cannot be found
questions.summary: BigQuery jobs are tied to a location; looking one up needs the job's location as well as its ID.
questions.question: A load job ran in the europe-west3 location. When you look it up by its job ID from a session whose default location is US, BigQuery reports that the job was not found, although you have permission to see it. What should you do?

options.A: Wait an hour, until job metadata is replicated globally.
options.B: Grant yourself BigQuery Admin on the project.
options.C: Look it up in Cloud Logging, since BigQuery deletes job records after an hour.
options.D: Look the job up again, giving its location, europe-west3.

explanation.summary: BigQuery jobs exist in a location. A lookup without the right location searches the default one and reports the job as not found.

option_breakdown.A: Job metadata isn't replicated across locations; waiting changes nothing.
option_breakdown.B: The problem is the location, not your permissions.
option_breakdown.C: Job history is kept far longer than an hour; the job is in another location.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. bq show -j --location=europe-west3 JOB_ID finds the job and its status.

questions.title: A CI gate on bytes scanned
questions.summary: A BigQuery dry run reports the bytes a query would process without running it, which a CI check can compare with a limit.
questions.question: A team keeps its dashboard SQL in Git. A CI check must reject any pull request whose changed queries would scan more than 1 TB, without executing them. What should the check do for each query?

options.A: Submit it as a dry run and compare the bytes reported with 1 TB.
options.B: Run it with LIMIT 10 and compare the bytes billed.
options.C: Run it fully in a sandbox project and read the job's statistics.
options.D: Compare the table's row count with a fixed row budget.

explanation.summary: On-demand queries are billed by bytes processed. A dry run validates the query and returns the bytes it would process, at no charge, which gives the cost.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. A dry run validates the query and returns the bytes it would process, without running it or incurring charges.
option_breakdown.B: LIMIT doesn't reduce the bytes scanned for most queries, and the query still runs.
option_breakdown.C: Running every query costs what the check is meant to prevent.
option_breakdown.D: Row counts don't say which columns a query reads or how many bytes that is.

explanation.gcloud_command: bq query --use_legacy_sql=false --dry_run 'SELECT user_id FROM `p.ds.events` WHERE day = "2026-10-01"'

questions.title: Tables nobody modifies any more
questions.summary: BigQuery bills tables or partitions unmodified for 90 consecutive days at the lower long-term storage price, automatically.
questions.question: Most tables in a BigQuery dataset are loaded once and never modified, though they are queried every week. Finance wants the storage estimate for next year to reflect that. What should the estimate assume?

options.A: Queries reset the tables to active storage, so the full active price applies.
options.B: The tables must be exported to Archive Storage to get any discount.
options.C: After 90 days without modification, the long-term storage price applies automatically.
options.D: Storage prices drop only after the dataset is moved to a multi-region.

explanation.summary: A table or partition not modified for 90 consecutive days is billed at the long-term storage price, roughly half the active price. Reading it doesn't change that.

option_breakdown.A: Querying doesn't count as modifying a table, so long-term pricing still applies.
option_breakdown.B: Long-term pricing applies inside BigQuery, with no export and no loss of performance.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Long-term pricing applies automatically to data unmodified for 90 days, even while it is queried.
option_breakdown.D: Location doesn't make data long-term; the 90 days without modification do.

explanation.gcloud_command: # Console > BigQuery > dataset > table > Details: Long-term storage bytes

questions.title: One switch for object-level permissions
questions.summary: Uniform bucket-level access disables ACLs so that access to every object is controlled by IAM alone.
questions.question: An audit of a bucket finds thousands of objects with individual ACLs granting access to various users, which nobody can review. Security wants access to every object in the bucket decided by IAM alone. What should you do?

options.A: Enable uniform bucket-level access on the bucket.
options.B: Set each object's ACL to private with a script.
options.C: Enable Object Versioning so old ACLs are archived.
options.D: Turn on soft delete with the longest retention.

explanation.summary: With uniform bucket-level access, ACLs no longer grant access and only IAM policies apply to the bucket and its objects. It can be turned off again within 90 days.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Uniform access makes IAM the only access control, so object ACLs stop mattering.
option_breakdown.B: A script fixes today's ACLs, but anyone with permission can add new ones tomorrow.
option_breakdown.C: Versioning keeps older object versions; it has no effect on who can read objects.
option_breakdown.D: Soft delete keeps deleted objects recoverable; it doesn't change access.

questions.title: A one-hour download link for an outsider
questions.summary: A signed URL grants time-limited access to one object to anyone who has the link, with no Google account needed.
questions.question: An auditor at an outside firm, who has no Google account, needs to fetch a single PDF from a private bucket this afternoon. The access must lapse by itself after sixty minutes and reveal nothing else. What should you send them?

options.A: An IAM grant of Storage Object Viewer to allUsers on the object.
options.B: Storage Object Viewer on the bucket for the customer's email address.
options.C: A signed URL for the object, valid for one hour.
options.D: A copy of the report in a new public bucket, deleted later.

explanation.summary: A signed URL carries its own time-limited authorisation for one object, so anyone with the link can download it until it expires, without a Google account.

option_breakdown.A: Public access never expires on its own and exposes the object to everyone.
option_breakdown.B: IAM needs a Google identity, which the customer doesn't have, and covers the whole bucket.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. The URL works for one object and stops working after an hour.
option_breakdown.D: A public bucket exposes the copy to everyone, and it depends on someone remembering to delete it.

questions.title: Sharing a custom image with another project
questions.summary: Granting Compute Image User on an image, or its project, lets principals elsewhere create VMs from it.
questions.question: The platform team publishes a hardened custom image in project images-prod. Developers in project app-dev must be able to create VMs from it, but not change or delete it. What should you grant the developers' group?

options.A: Compute Instance Admin on images-prod.
options.B: Storage Object Viewer on the image's Cloud Storage bucket.
options.C: Owner on images-prod, limited by an IAM condition.
options.D: Compute Image User on the image in images-prod.

explanation.summary: Compute Image User allows using an image to create disks and VMs, without permission to modify or delete it. Granted on the image, it shares only that image.

option_breakdown.A: Instance Admin lets them manage VMs in images-prod, which isn't the need, and doesn't cover using the image from app-dev.
option_breakdown.B: Custom images aren't stored as objects you can grant access to.
option_breakdown.C: Owner allows changing and deleting everything, and conditions can't be used with basic roles.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. It lets the group use the image from their own project, and nothing more.

questions.title: Credentials for a new Windows VM
questions.summary: gcloud compute reset-windows-password creates or resets a local Windows account and returns its password.
questions.question: You've just created a Windows Server VM from a public image and can reach it over RDP. You don't have any Windows credentials for it yet. What should you do?

options.A: Use your Google account's password at the Windows sign-in.
options.B: Add an SSH public key to the VM's metadata and use it for RDP.
options.C: Generate a Windows password for a local account with gcloud or the console.
options.D: Read the Administrator password from the serial port output.

explanation.summary: For Windows VMs, Compute Engine can create a local user and set a password for it (gcloud compute reset-windows-password, or Set Windows password in the console), which you then use for RDP.

option_breakdown.A: Windows on the VM doesn't know your Google account; RDP needs a local or domain account.
option_breakdown.B: RDP doesn't use SSH keys.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. The command creates or resets the account and returns a generated password.
option_breakdown.D: The serial port output doesn't show an Administrator password; generating one is the supported route.

questions.title: A CPU-heavy service drowning in parallel requests
questions.summary: Lowering concurrency on a CPU-bound Cloud Run service makes it add instances instead of overloading each one.
questions.question: A Cloud Run service resizes images; each request uses a whole vCPU for about a second. With the default concurrency, latency climbs badly under load, although the service is far below its maximum instances. What should you change?

options.A: Lower the concurrency to about one request per vCPU.
options.B: Raise the concurrency so each instance takes more requests.
options.C: Set a request timeout of 60 minutes.
options.D: Lower the maximum number of instances.

explanation.summary: Cloud Run scales out when instances reach their concurrency. A CPU-bound handler can't serve many requests at once, so lower concurrency makes Cloud Run add instances instead of queueing work on busy CPUs.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. With concurrency near the vCPU count, requests spread across more instances.
option_breakdown.B: More concurrent requests per instance make the CPU contention worse.
option_breakdown.C: A longer timeout lets slow requests run longer; it doesn't make them faster.
option_breakdown.D: Fewer instances concentrate the load further.

questions.title: Querying CSV files where they already are
questions.summary: A BigQuery external table queries files in Cloud Storage in place, without loading them.
questions.question: Partners drop CSV files into a Cloud Storage bucket every hour. Analysts want to query all of them with SQL in BigQuery, always including the newest files, without building a load pipeline. What should you create?

options.A: A load job scheduled every hour into a native table.
options.B: A Dataflow pipeline that streams the files into BigQuery.
options.C: A BigQuery external table over the bucket's CSV files.
options.D: A Cloud SQL instance that imports the files.

explanation.summary: An external table points BigQuery at files in Cloud Storage, so queries read whatever files match its URI pattern at query time, with no loading step.

option_breakdown.A: Scheduled loads are a pipeline to run, and results lag by up to an hour.
option_breakdown.B: Dataflow is a pipeline to build and pay for.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. New files matching the URI wildcard are included in the next query.
option_breakdown.D: Cloud SQL adds a database and an import process for data BigQuery can read directly.

questions.title: Configuration-change records for three years
questions.summary: Admin Activity logs stay 400 days in the _Required bucket; longer retention needs a sink to a destination you control.
questions.question: Auditors will ask for records of who changed which resource, going back three years. Today those records exist only where Google Cloud writes them by default, which keeps them for just over a year. What should you set up?

options.A: Raise the retention of the bucket where they are written by default.
options.B: Create a sink that routes the audit logs to a bucket with three-year retention.
options.C: Enable Data Access audit logs, which keep Admin Activity entries longer.
options.D: Export the logs to a spreadsheet each quarter.

explanation.summary: The _Required bucket keeps Admin Activity logs for 400 days, and that can't be changed. A sink can also route them to a log bucket, or a Cloud Storage bucket, with the retention you need.

option_breakdown.A: Admin Activity logs land in the _Required bucket, whose 400-day retention can't be changed.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. The sink sends a copy to a destination whose retention you set to three years.
option_breakdown.C: Data Access logs are different entries, and they don't extend anything's retention.
option_breakdown.D: Manual exports are error-prone and lose the logs' structure.

questions.title: Settings and a password for the same Pods
questions.summary: Keep non-sensitive configuration in a ConfigMap and credentials in a Secret, both outside the image, and reference them from the Pod spec.
questions.question: A GKE Deployment at Ruthin Tools needs a feature-flag file and a database password. Neither may be baked into the container image, the flags change weekly without a rebuild, and the password must not be stored in plain text in the Deployment manifest. Which two actions should you take? (Choose two.)

options.A: Store the feature flags in a ConfigMap mounted into the Pods.
options.B: Put the password in an environment variable written in the Deployment manifest.
options.C: Store the flags as annotations on the Deployment object.
options.D: Store the password in a Kubernetes Secret and reference it from the Pod spec.
options.E: Copy both into the image at build time.

explanation.summary: ConfigMaps hold configuration that Pods read as files or variables, and can be changed without a new image. Secrets hold credentials separately from the manifests that use them.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. The flags change weekly by updating the ConfigMap, with no rebuild.
option_breakdown.B: The password would sit in plain text in the manifest, which is ruled out.
option_breakdown.C: Annotations are metadata for tools, not a way to hand configuration to containers.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. The manifest references the Secret by name, and the value lives elsewhere.
option_breakdown.E: Both would be baked into the image, which is forbidden.

explanation.gcloud_command:
kubectl create configmap flags --from-file=flags.yaml
kubectl create secret generic db --from-literal=password=REDACTED

questions.title: No cold starts, and a cap on Cloud Run cost
questions.summary: Minimum instances keep instances warm to avoid cold starts; maximum instances cap how far the service scales out.
questions.question: Customers of Penrose Bank notice slow first requests on a Cloud Run API in the morning, and a traffic spike last month also ran up an unexpected bill and overloaded the database behind it. The service must stay warm, and scale out to no more than 20 instances. Which two settings should you change? (Choose two.)

options.A: Set the minimum number of instances to 1.
options.B: Switch to a larger CPU allocation for each instance.
options.C: Set the request timeout to 60 minutes.
options.D: Set the maximum concurrent requests per instance to 1.
options.E: Set the maximum number of instances to 20.

explanation.summary: With a minimum of one instance, Cloud Run keeps an instance ready, so the first request doesn't wait for a cold start. A maximum of 20 caps scale-out, which bounds both the cost and the connections to the database.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. A warm instance removes the morning cold start.
option_breakdown.B: More CPU may speed start-up slightly, but it neither keeps an instance warm nor caps scale.
option_breakdown.C: A longer timeout lets requests run longer; it doesn't avoid cold starts or limit scale.
option_breakdown.D: Concurrency of 1 makes Cloud Run start more instances, which worsens both cost and database load.
option_breakdown.E: Correct. The service never runs more than 20 instances.

questions.title: Upgrading nodes without dropping below two replicas
questions.summary: Surge upgrades with maxUnavailable 0 add a new node before draining an old one, and a PodDisruptionBudget stops drains from evicting too many replicas at once.
questions.question: Hexham Energy is upgrading a GKE Standard node pool that runs a three-replica payment service. During the upgrade, at least two replicas must stay running at all times, and no node may be drained before its replacement exists. Which two actions should you take? (Choose two.)

options.A: Scale the payment Deployment down to one replica for the upgrade window.
options.B: Set the node pool's surge upgrade to maxSurge 1 and maxUnavailable 0.
options.C: Create a PodDisruptionBudget for the service with minAvailable set to 2.
options.D: Turn off node auto-repair on the pool until the upgrade finishes.
options.E: Delete the node pool, then create a new one on the target version.

explanation.summary: Surge settings control how nodes are replaced: maxSurge 1 with maxUnavailable 0 creates a new node before cordoning and draining an old one. GKE respects PodDisruptionBudgets when draining, so no more than one replica is evicted at a time.

option_breakdown.A: One replica means the service is down while that Pod moves.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. A replacement node exists before any old node is drained.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Drains wait rather than let fewer than two replicas run.
option_breakdown.D: Auto-repair is unrelated to how upgrades replace nodes.
option_breakdown.E: Deleting the pool evicts every replica at once.

questions.title: A Cloud SQL database that survives a region outage
questions.summary: For regional disaster recovery on Cloud SQL, keep a cross-region read replica to promote, and store backups in a location outside the primary region.
questions.question: Kirby Hotels' booking database is a Cloud SQL for MySQL instance with high availability in us-east1. Management wants it back within an hour if the whole region becomes unavailable, and backups that don't depend on that region. Which two actions should you take? (Choose two.)

options.A: Take on-demand backups more often, and keep them in us-east1.
options.B: Create a cross-region read replica in us-central1, ready to promote.
options.C: Turn on query insights for the instance to watch its health.
options.D: Store automated backups in a custom location outside us-east1.
options.E: Rely on the HA standby that runs in another zone of us-east1.

explanation.summary: High availability protects against a zone failure only. A cross-region replica can be promoted to a standalone primary if the region is lost, and backups stored in another location remain usable when the primary region isn't.

option_breakdown.A: More frequent backups still in us-east1 are lost with the region.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Promoting the replica brings the database back in another region quickly.
option_breakdown.C: Query insights helps tune queries; it does nothing for recovery.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Backups in another location don't depend on us-east1.
option_breakdown.E: The HA standby is in the same region, so a regional outage takes both down.

questions.title: Proving which firewall rule allowed a connection
questions.summary: Firewall Rules Logging records each connection a rule allows or denies, and the entries are read in Cloud Logging.
questions.question: From now on, auditors at Sandford Water must be able to see which VPC firewall rule allowed each connection to a reporting VM on TCP 8443. Several overlapping allow rules exist. Which two actions should you take? (Choose two.)

options.A: Enable Data Access audit logs for Compute Engine.
options.B: Turn on logging for the candidate allow rules.
options.C: Create an uptime check for port 8443.
options.D: Delete the overlapping rules and recreate one rule.
options.E: Query the firewall log entries for the VM in the Logs Explorer.

explanation.summary: With Firewall Rules Logging on, each connection a rule matches produces a log entry that names the rule. The entries are in Cloud Logging, where you can filter by VM and port. Logging starts when you enable it, so past connections aren't covered.

option_breakdown.A: Data Access audit logs record API calls, not network connections.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Logging records which rule matched each new connection from now on.
option_breakdown.C: An uptime check tests reachability; it doesn't say which rule allowed it.
option_breakdown.D: Deleting rules changes the configuration and doesn't show which one allowed traffic.
option_breakdown.E: Correct. The entries name the rule that matched each connection.

questions.title: Apache logs and metrics from a VM fleet
questions.summary: The Ops Agent collects system metrics and logs, and its configuration file adds receivers for third-party applications such as Apache.
questions.question: Aldbury Books runs Apache on 40 Compute Engine VMs. Operations needs memory and disk metrics, Apache's request metrics, and Apache's access and error logs, all in Cloud Monitoring and Cloud Logging. Which two actions should you take? (Choose two.)

options.A: Enable VPC Flow Logs on the VMs' subnet.
options.B: Turn on Data Access audit logs for Compute Engine.
options.C: Install the Ops Agent on the VMs.
options.D: Add Apache receivers for metrics and logs to the Ops Agent configuration.
options.E: Create a log sink that routes syslog to BigQuery.

explanation.summary: The Ops Agent sends guest metrics, such as memory and disk, and system logs. Third-party applications need receivers in the agent's config.yaml, and Apache has receivers for both its metrics and its logs.

option_breakdown.A: Flow logs show network traffic, not Apache metrics or logs.
option_breakdown.B: Audit logs record API calls, not what Apache serves.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. The agent provides memory, disk and system logs from inside the VMs.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. The Apache receivers add its request metrics and its access and error logs.
option_breakdown.E: A sink routes logs that are already collected; it doesn't collect Apache's logs.

explanation.gcloud_command:
# /etc/google-cloud-ops-agent/config.yaml: metrics receiver type apache, logging receivers apache_access and apache_error
sudo systemctl restart google-cloud-ops-agent

questions.title: Logs for analysis now and a cheap archive for years
questions.summary: Use one sink to BigQuery for SQL analysis and another to a Cloud Storage bucket for long, low-cost retention.
questions.question: Compliance at Elmswell Bank wants application logs available for SQL analysis for 90 days, and an archive of the same logs kept for seven years at the lowest storage cost. Both must fill automatically as logs arrive. Which two actions should you take? (Choose two.)

options.A: Create a log-based metric for every application log the services write.
options.B: Export the logs by hand from the Logs Explorer at the end of each month.
options.C: Sink to a Cloud Storage bucket with a lifecycle rule to Archive.
options.D: Extend the _Default log bucket's retention period to seven years.
options.E: Create a sink to a BigQuery dataset whose tables expire after 90 days.

explanation.summary: Sinks route matching logs as they arrive. A BigQuery destination gives SQL analysis; a Cloud Storage destination with a lifecycle rule to Archive is the cheapest long-term store.

option_breakdown.A: Metrics count logs; they don't keep the log contents.
option_breakdown.B: Manual exports aren't automatic and will be missed.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. The bucket keeps seven years cheaply, and the rule moves objects to Archive.
option_breakdown.D: Long retention in a log bucket costs more per GB than Archive storage.
option_breakdown.E: Correct. Logs land in BigQuery for SQL, and table expiry drops them after 90 days.

questions.title: Signing in to a new Windows VM through IAP
questions.summary: A Windows VM needs a generated Windows password, and with IAP TCP forwarding, port 3389 opened to IAP's range.
questions.question: An engineer at Ludlow Clinics created a Windows Server VM with no external IP address and must connect to it with Remote Desktop from a laptop, using IAP TCP forwarding. The VPC allows only internal traffic, and the engineer already has IAP-secured Tunnel User. Which two actions should you take? (Choose two.)

options.A: Add the engineer's SSH public key to the VM's metadata.
options.B: Give the VM an ephemeral external IP address for the session.
options.C: Enable OS Login on the VM through its instance metadata.
options.D: Generate a Windows password for the engineer's user on the VM.
options.E: Allow ingress on TCP 3389 from 35.235.240.0/20 to the VM.

explanation.summary: Windows VMs use a username and password for RDP, which Compute Engine can generate. IAP's forwarders connect from 35.235.240.0/20, so port 3389 must be open to that range.

option_breakdown.A: SSH keys are for Linux SSH, not for RDP to Windows.
option_breakdown.B: An external IP isn't needed with IAP and would expose the VM.
option_breakdown.C: OS Login controls SSH access to Linux VMs, not RDP to Windows.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. A generated password is how the engineer signs in to Windows.
option_breakdown.E: Correct. IAP reaches the VM's RDP port from this range.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud compute reset-windows-password win-1 --zone=ZONE --user=engineer
gcloud compute start-iap-tunnel win-1 3389 --local-host-port=localhost:3389 --zone=ZONE

questions.title: Knowing a query's cost before running it
questions.summary: A dry run, or the console's query validator, reports the bytes a query would process without running it; on-demand cost follows from those bytes.
questions.question: Kinver Media's analysts pay on-demand BigQuery prices. Before launching a heavy join against two years of clickstream tables, an analyst wants the number of bytes it will scan, and finding that out must itself cost nothing. Which two approaches give that number? (Choose two.)

options.A: Read the bytes-processed estimate in the console's query validator.
options.B: Run the query with the --dry_run flag in the bq tool.
options.C: Run the query with LIMIT 10 added, and multiply the cost it shows.
options.D: Check the table's storage size in the Cloud Billing reports page.
options.E: Run the full query and cancel it after a few seconds of processing.

explanation.summary: A dry run validates a query and returns the bytes it would process, at no charge. The console's validator shows the same estimate while you type. On-demand pricing then follows from bytes processed.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. The validator shows the estimate before you run anything.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. A dry run is free and returns the bytes processed.
option_breakdown.C: LIMIT doesn't reduce bytes scanned, so the small query costs as much as the full one.
option_breakdown.D: Storage size doesn't tell you which columns and partitions the query reads.
option_breakdown.E: A cancelled query may still be charged for the work done.

explanation.gcloud_command: bq query --use_legacy_sql=false --dry_run 'SELECT user_id FROM media.events WHERE day = "2026-11-01"'

questions.title: A vendor's allow-list and a NAT address that changed
questions.summary: Automatic NAT IP allocation can add or change addresses; manual assignment of reserved static IPs keeps egress on fixed addresses.
questions.question: Report servers at Harwell Logistics have no external IP addresses and upload files to a vendor's SFTP server through Cloud NAT, which uses automatic IP allocation. After the NAT gateway added an address during a busy week, the vendor started rejecting some uploads, because it accepts only the addresses on its allow-list. What should you change?

options.A: Give each report server an ephemeral external IP address.
options.B: Enable Private Google Access on the report servers' subnet.
options.C: Switch the NAT gateway to manual assignment of reserved static IPs.
options.D: Add a route to the vendor's range through the default internet gateway.

explanation.summary: With automatic allocation, Cloud NAT chooses and can add addresses as demand grows. Manual assignment uses only the static addresses you reserved, so the vendor can allow-list exactly those.

option_breakdown.A: Ephemeral external addresses change when VMs are recreated, and the vendor would need every one of them.
option_breakdown.B: Private Google Access reaches Google APIs only, not a vendor's SFTP server on the internet.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Manual NAT IP assignment sends all translated traffic from the reserved static addresses, which never change.
option_breakdown.D: A route decides where packets go, not which source address they carry; without NAT the VMs can't reach the internet at all.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud compute addresses create nat-ip-1 nat-ip-2 --region=R
gcloud compute routers nats update nat-1 --router=nat-router --region=R \
  --nat-external-ip-pool=nat-ip-1,nat-ip-2

questions.title: Cloud NAT that works in one region only
questions.summary: Cloud NAT is regional: each region with private VMs that need internet egress needs its own Cloud Router and NAT gateway.
questions.question: A VPC network at Sefton Analytics has subnets in us-central1 and europe-west1. Its VMs have no external IP addresses. A Cloud Router with a Cloud NAT gateway covering all subnet ranges exists in us-central1. VMs in us-central1 download packages from the internet, but VMs in europe-west1 time out. What should you do?

options.A: Create a Cloud Router and a Cloud NAT gateway in europe-west1.
options.B: Set the VPC network's dynamic routing mode to global.
options.C: Add a static route in europe-west1 with the us-central1 NAT gateway as next hop.
options.D: Raise the minimum ports per VM on the existing NAT gateway.

explanation.summary: A Cloud NAT gateway serves subnets in its own region only, even when it is set to cover all subnet ranges. The europe-west1 VMs need a gateway in europe-west1.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Cloud NAT is regional, so a second Cloud Router and NAT gateway in europe-west1 gives those VMs egress.
option_breakdown.B: The dynamic routing mode affects routes learned over BGP, not which region a NAT gateway serves.
option_breakdown.C: A NAT gateway is not a VM or load balancer that a static route can use as its next hop.
option_breakdown.D: More ports help a region that already has NAT and drops connections; europe-west1 has no NAT at all.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud compute routers create nat-router-euw1 --network=NETWORK --region=europe-west1
gcloud compute routers nats create nat-euw1 --router=nat-router-euw1 --region=europe-west1 \
  --nat-all-subnet-ip-ranges --auto-allocate-nat-external-ips

questions.title: Keeping a load balancer's current address before a rebuild
questions.summary: An in-use ephemeral external address can be promoted to a static address, so a rebuilt load balancer can keep the exact IP customers already allow-list.
questions.question: A global external Application Load Balancer at Brockley Tickets was created with an ephemeral IP address, and hundreds of customers have that address in their firewall allow-lists.
