Next week you will delete and recreate the load balancer's forwarding rule. Customers must not have to change anything. What should you do first?

options.A: Reserve a new global static external IP address for the new forwarding rule.
options.B: Promote the forwarding rule's current ephemeral address to a global static address.
options.C: Promote the current address to a regional static address in the backends' region.
options.D: Publish the load balancer's address in Cloud DNS and ask customers to use the name.

explanation.summary: Promoting an in-use ephemeral address reserves that same address as static. It then survives the forwarding rule's deletion and can be attached to the new one.

option_breakdown.A: A newly reserved address is a different IP, so every customer would have to update its allow-list.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Promoting the current ephemeral address keeps the exact IP, now reserved, ready for the new forwarding rule.
option_breakdown.C: A global load balancer uses global addresses; a regional static address can't be attached to it.
option_breakdown.D: Customers allow-list an IP address in their firewalls, so a DNS name doesn't remove the change for them.

questions.title: A VM whose public address changed after a restart
questions.summary: A VM needs a reserved regional static external address to keep its public IP through stops and replacement; global addresses are for global load balancers.
questions.question: A licence server on a Compute Engine VM in europe-west2 is reached by desktop clients at its public IP address. After a maintenance stop and start, the address changed and every client failed to connect. The VM will also be replaced by a new one next quarter. What should you do so the address stays the same?

options.A: Reserve a global static external IP address and assign it to the VM.
options.B: Reserve a static internal IP address in the VM's subnet.
options.C: Bring your own IP range to Google Cloud and assign an address from it.
options.D: Reserve a regional static external IP address and assign it to the VM.

explanation.summary: A VM's ephemeral external address is released when it stops. A reserved regional static external address stays in the project and can be moved to the replacement VM.

option_breakdown.A: Global addresses are for global load balancers; a VM's external address is regional.
option_breakdown.B: An internal address isn't reachable by clients on the internet.
option_breakdown.C: Bringing your own range works but is a heavy process for owned address blocks, far beyond keeping one address.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. A reserved regional static external address survives stops and is reassigned to the new VM when it replaces this one.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud compute addresses create licence-ip --region=europe-west2
gcloud compute instances add-access-config licence-vm --zone=ZONE --address=ADDRESS

questions.title: Where on-premises DNS sends queries for a private zone
questions.summary: An inbound server policy allocates entry-point addresses in the VPC's subnets; on-premises resolvers forward the private zone's domain to them.
questions.question: You created an inbound DNS server policy on the VPC network that Kestrel Bank's data centre reaches over HA VPN in europe-west4. The on-premises DNS team now asks which addresses to forward queries for the private zone svc.kestrel.internal to. What should you give them?

options.A: The metadata server address, 169.254.169.254.
options.B: The inbound forwarder addresses the policy allocated in the europe-west4 subnets.
options.C: The range 35.199.192.0/19, which Cloud DNS uses for forwarding.
options.D: Google Public DNS at 8.8.8.8 and 8.8.4.4.

explanation.summary: An inbound server policy reserves an address in each subnet of the VPC as an entry point. On-premises resolvers forward to the entry points in the region their connection lands in, and get answers from the VPC's private zones.

option_breakdown.A: The metadata server answers only VMs inside Google Cloud, not traffic arriving over a VPN.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. The policy's inbound forwarder addresses in europe-west4, where the VPN lands, are what on-premises DNS forwards to.
option_breakdown.C: 35.199.192.0/19 is the source of Cloud DNS's outbound forwarding queries, the opposite direction.
option_breakdown.D: Public DNS can't see a private zone, which is visible only to authorised VPC networks.

questions.title: A forwarding zone whose answers never arrive
questions.summary: Cloud DNS sends forwarded queries from 35.199.192.0/19 over the hybrid connection, so on-premises firewalls and routes must allow that range.
questions.question: VMs at Pendle Insurance must resolve names in corp.pendle.example, which only on-premises DNS servers hold. You created a Cloud DNS forwarding zone for that domain targeting the on-premises servers' private addresses over Cloud Interconnect, but every query times out. The on-premises firewall logs show dropped packets. What should the network team allow?

options.A: DNS traffic from the VMs' subnet ranges to the on-premises servers.
options.B: DNS traffic from Google's health-check ranges 35.191.0.0/16 and 130.211.0.0/22.
options.C: DNS traffic from the range 35.199.192.0/19 to the on-premises servers.
options.D: DNS traffic from the metadata server address 169.254.169.254.

explanation.summary: Queries sent through a forwarding zone to private targets come from Cloud DNS's own range, 35.199.192.0/19, not from the VMs. On-premises must accept that range and route replies back over the hybrid link.

option_breakdown.A: The VMs ask Cloud DNS; the forwarded query leaves from Cloud DNS's range, not the VMs' addresses.
option_breakdown.B: Those ranges send load-balancer health checks, not DNS queries.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Cloud DNS forwards from 35.199.192.0/19, which the on-premises firewall must allow and route back through Interconnect.
option_breakdown.D: The metadata server address is link-local inside Google Cloud and never appears on-premises.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud dns managed-zones create corp-fwd --dns-name=corp.pendle.example. --visibility=private \
  --networks=NETWORK --forwarding-targets=10.20.0.53,10.20.0.54 --description='to on-premises'

questions.title: An Autopilot cluster that ran out of Pod addresses
questions.summary: Autopilot clusters on GKE 1.26 and later can take additional Pod IPv4 ranges from new subnet secondary ranges, used for nodes in new node pools.
questions.question: An Autopilot cluster on GKE 1.31 at Fenwick Mobile can't schedule new Pods because its Pod IPv4 range is exhausted. The address space next to the range is used by another subnet. The cluster must keep running and keep its name. What should you do?

options.A: Expand the subnet's primary range with expand-ip-range.
options.B: Recreate the cluster as a Standard cluster with a larger Pod range.
options.C: Add a subnet secondary range and assign it to the cluster as an additional Pod range.
options.D: Lower the cluster's maximum Pods per node in place.

explanation.summary: Additional Pod IPv4 ranges come from new, discontiguous subnet secondary ranges. Autopilot (1.26 and later) uses them for Pod addresses on the nodes it creates next, with no cluster rebuild.

option_breakdown.A: The primary range holds node addresses; Pod addresses come from secondary ranges, so expanding it doesn't help.
option_breakdown.B: Recreating the cluster is the disruption the stem rules out, and Autopilot supports additional ranges anyway.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. A new secondary range added as an additional Pod range gives new nodes Pod addresses without recreating anything.
option_breakdown.D: Autopilot manages Pods per node, and changing it in place isn't possible on existing nodes.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud compute networks subnets update SUBNET --region=R --add-secondary-ranges=pods-2=10.96.0.0/16
gcloud container clusters update fenwick --location=R --additional-pod-ipv4-ranges=pods-2

questions.title: How many secondary ranges one subnet can hold
questions.summary: A subnet can have up to 170 secondary IPv4 ranges, a limit that can't be raised; ranges must not overlap anything else in the VPC.
questions.question: The platform team at Glenrothes Data gives each new GKE node pool its own Pod range, all taken from secondary ranges on one shared subnet. They ask what eventually limits this design. What should you tell them?

options.A: A subnet can have at most two secondary ranges, one for Pods and one for Services.
options.B: There is no limit, as long as the ranges don't overlap.
options.C: A quota on secondary ranges that support can raise as far as needed.
options.D: A subnet can hold up to 170 secondary ranges, and that limit can't be increased.

explanation.summary: Each subnet supports up to 170 secondary IPv4 ranges, and the limit can't be increased. The ranges must also stay clear of every other range in the VPC and its peers.

option_breakdown.A: A VPC-native cluster starts with one Pod and one Service range, but a subnet can hold many more secondary ranges.
option_breakdown.B: The number per subnet is capped, and the VPC's total subnet ranges are limited too.
option_breakdown.C: The per-subnet maximum is a fixed limit, not an adjustable quota.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Up to 170 secondary ranges per subnet, a hard limit, so very many node pools eventually need another subnet.

explanation.gcloud_command: gcloud compute networks subnets describe SUBNET --region=R --format='value(secondaryIpRanges)'

questions.title: Using a workstation someone else created
questions.summary: The Cloud Workstations User role on a workstation lets a person start and use it; creating workstations needs the Creator role on a configuration.
questions.question: A platform administrator at Hexley Games created a workstation named ana-dev from the configuration unity-dev for a contractor. The contractor must be able to start and use that one workstation, but not create others or change the configuration. What should you grant?

options.A: roles/workstations.workstationCreator on the unity-dev configuration.
options.B: roles/workstations.admin on the project.
options.C: roles/workstations.operationViewer on the project.
options.D: roles/workstations.user on the ana-dev workstation.

explanation.summary: Cloud Workstations User on a workstation lets someone start, stop and connect to it, and nothing else.

option_breakdown.A: Creator lets the contractor create new workstations from the configuration, which isn't wanted.
option_breakdown.B: Admin controls clusters and configurations, far more than using one workstation.
option_breakdown.C: Operation Viewer shows long-running operations, not access to a workstation.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. The User role on that workstation is exactly enough to start and use it.

questions.title: Counting errors from a log field
questions.summary: A counter log-based metric counts matching log entries, which is how an error rate is charted and alerted on; distribution metrics are for numeric values such as latency.
questions.question: A legacy service at Wrexham Bus writes one structured log entry per request with jsonPayload.status. The team wants to chart and alert on the number of requests with status 500 per minute, without changing code. What should it create?

options.A: A distribution log-based metric on jsonPayload.status.
options.B: An uptime check against the service's health endpoint.
options.C: A counter log-based metric for entries with jsonPayload.status=500.
options.D: A log sink to BigQuery with a query scheduled every minute.

explanation.summary: A counter log-based metric counts the entries that match its filter, giving a time series of 500s per minute for charts and alerting policies.

option_breakdown.A: A distribution summarises a numeric value's spread; the team wants a count of matching requests.
option_breakdown.B: An uptime check probes one endpoint and doesn't count the errors real users get.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. A counter metric with the filter jsonPayload.status=500 is the error count to chart and alert on.
option_breakdown.D: A scheduled query adds delay and cost, and alerting on it needs more plumbing.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud logging metrics create http-500 --description='500 responses' \
  --log-filter='resource.type="gce_instance" AND jsonPayload.status=500'

questions.title: Latency hidden in a plain-text log line
questions.summary: A distribution log-based metric can extract a number from textPayload with a regular expression, and percentiles are charted from the resulting histogram.
questions.question: An old service at Kirkby Freight writes plain-text log lines such as "GET /quote done in 238ms". There is no latency metric, and the code can't change. The team wants p95 latency on a dashboard. What should it create?

options.A: A distribution log-based metric that extracts the number before ms with a regular expression.
options.B: A counter log-based metric for entries containing done in.
options.C: A metric-absence alert on the service's request logs.
options.D: A log bucket with Log Analytics, queried by hand each morning.

explanation.summary: Distribution metrics take a value extractor, which may be a regular expression over textPayload. The extracted numbers form a histogram that Cloud Monitoring turns into percentiles.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. A regex extractor on textPayload captures the milliseconds, and the distribution gives p95 on a chart.
option_breakdown.B: A counter counts requests but discards the latency value.
option_breakdown.C: Metric absence detects silence, not slowness.
option_breakdown.D: Manual queries produce numbers each morning, not a live percentile chart.

explanation.gcloud_command: # Logs-based metric > Distribution > Field: textPayload, Regular expression: done in (\d+)ms

questions.title: A sink into another project's bucket that writes nothing
questions.summary: A sink writes as its writer identity, which needs a role on the destination: for a Cloud Storage bucket, Storage Object Creator.
questions.question: A log sink in project web-prod at Ashby Telecom routes firewall logs to the Cloud Storage bucket fw-archive in project sec-archive. The sink was created without errors, but the bucket stays empty after a day. What should you do?

options.A: Grant your own account Storage Admin on the bucket.
options.B: Grant the sink's writer identity Storage Object Creator on the bucket.
options.C: Recreate the sink in project sec-archive.
options.D: Enable Data Access audit logs for Cloud Storage in sec-archive.

explanation.summary: Sinks write with their own writer identity. When the destination is in another project, that identity must be granted permission there, here Storage Object Creator on the bucket.

option_breakdown.A: Your account doesn't write the logs; the sink's writer identity does.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. The writer identity needs Storage Object Creator on fw-archive before routed entries are written.
option_breakdown.C: A sink routes logs of the project it lives in, so moving it would route sec-archive's logs instead.
option_breakdown.D: Data Access logs record reads of the bucket; they don't let the sink write.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud logging sinks describe fw-to-archive --project=web-prod --format='value(writerIdentity)'
gcloud storage buckets add-iam-policy-binding gs://fw-archive --member=WRITER_IDENTITY --role=roles/storage.objectCreator

questions.title: A PodMonitoring resource in the wrong namespace
questions.summary: PodMonitoring is namespaced and selects Pods only in its own namespace; ClusterPodMonitoring selects across namespaces.
questions.question: On a GKE cluster at Morley Cars with Managed Service for Prometheus managed collection, the checkout Pods run in namespace shop and expose /metrics on port 8080. An engineer created a PodMonitoring resource selecting app=checkout in namespace default. No checkout metrics arrive. What should you do?

options.A: Install the Ops Agent on the cluster's nodes.
options.B: Rename the metrics port in the Pods to metrics.
options.C: Create the PodMonitoring resource in namespace shop.
options.D: Disable managed collection and run a Prometheus server.

explanation.summary: A PodMonitoring resource scrapes only Pods in its own namespace. The checkout Pods are in shop, so the resource must be there, or a ClusterPodMonitoring must be used.

option_breakdown.A: The Ops Agent is for VMs; GKE metrics from Prometheus endpoints come through managed collection.
option_breakdown.B: A port can be named anything, as long as the PodMonitoring refers to it correctly.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. In namespace shop the selector finds the checkout Pods and scraping starts.
option_breakdown.D: Managed collection works; it is only looking in the wrong namespace.

questions.title: Health metrics for self-managed MySQL on VMs
questions.summary: The Ops Agent's MySQL integration collects MySQL metrics and logs from Compute Engine VMs into Cloud Monitoring and Cloud Logging, using generally available features.
questions.question: Besides Cloud SQL, Tolland Retail runs self-managed MySQL on six Compute Engine VMs. The DBA lead wants their connections, query rates and slow-query logs in Cloud Monitoring and Cloud Logging, using only generally available features. What should you set up?

options.A: Migrate the six databases to Cloud SQL first.
options.B: Uptime checks against port 3306 on each VM.
options.C: VPC Flow Logs for the VMs' subnet.
options.D: The Ops Agent with its MySQL integration on each VM.

explanation.summary: The Ops Agent has a MySQL integration that collects the server's metrics and its error and slow-query logs, sending them to Cloud Monitoring and Cloud Logging.

option_breakdown.A: Migration may come later, but the lead wants the existing databases monitored now.
option_breakdown.B: An uptime check only says whether the port answers.
option_breakdown.C: Flow logs show network flows, not database metrics or logs.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. The agent's MySQL receiver collects metrics and logs from each VM.

explanation.gcloud_command: # /etc/google-cloud-ops-agent/config.yaml: metrics receiver type mysql, logs receivers mysql_error and mysql_slow

questions.title: Serial console refused by policy
questions.summary: The interactive serial console needs serial-port-enable on the VM or project, and the compute.disableSerialPortAccess organisation policy must not be enforced on it.
questions.question: A VM at Halton Water lost all network connectivity after a bad configuration change. You set serial-port-enable=TRUE in its metadata, but connecting to the serial console is still refused. The project sits in a folder where security policies are enforced. What should you check?

options.A: Whether the VM has an external IP address.
options.B: Whether a firewall rule allows 35.235.240.0/20 on port 22.
options.C: Whether the compute.disableSerialPortAccess policy is enforced on the project.
options.D: Whether OS Login is enabled in the project's metadata.

explanation.summary: The serial console goes through Compute Engine, not the VM's network, but the compute.disableSerialPortAccess organisation policy can forbid it regardless of the metadata.

option_breakdown.A: Serial console access doesn't use the VM's network or its addresses.
option_breakdown.B: That rule is for IAP TCP forwarding; the serial console doesn't pass through the VPC firewall.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. If the policy is enforced, serial port access is blocked whatever the metadata says.
option_breakdown.D: OS Login affects SSH and serial console sign-in, but it doesn't refuse the connection outright.

questions.title: Reading why a VM doesn't finish booting
questions.summary: Serial port output shows a VM's boot and kernel messages without signing in, which is the first look at a VM that won't boot.
questions.question: After a kernel update, a VM at Bexley Clinics shows as RUNNING but never becomes reachable. You want to read the boot messages to see where it stops, without changing anything on the VM. What should you do?

options.A: SSH to the VM through Identity-Aware Proxy.
options.B: Read the VM's serial port output.
options.C: Create a snapshot and attach it to another VM.
options.D: Install the Ops Agent and read its logs.

explanation.summary: Serial port 1 receives boot and kernel messages. Reading its output needs no sign-in, network or change to the VM.

option_breakdown.A: SSH needs a booted system with working networking, which this VM may not have.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. get-serial-port-output shows the boot log and where it stops.
option_breakdown.C: Mounting a snapshot elsewhere works for repairs, but it is slower than reading the output that already exists.
option_breakdown.D: An agent can't be installed or report on a VM that hasn't finished booting.

questions.title: A bigger machine type for every VM in a group
questions.summary: A managed instance group's machine type comes from its instance template; changing it means a new template and a rolling update, not editing each VM.
questions.question: The 12 VMs of a regional managed instance group at Grayson Online use e2-standard-4 and need e2-standard-8. The service must keep serving while the change happens. What should you do?

options.A: Stop each VM, change its machine type, and start it again.
options.B: Edit the existing instance template's machine type in place.
options.C: Create a template with e2-standard-8 and start a rolling update to it.
options.D: Resize the group to 24 VMs so the load halves.

explanation.summary: VMs in a managed group are built from the group's template. A new template with the larger machine type and a rolling update replace VMs a few at a time while the rest serve.

option_breakdown.A: The group would recreate or repair VMs back to the template; individual edits don't last.
option_breakdown.B: Instance templates can't be edited; a change needs a new template.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. A new template and a rolling update change every VM without stopping the service.
option_breakdown.D: More small VMs isn't the larger machine type the workload needs, and it costs more.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud compute instance-templates create web-e2-8 --machine-type=e2-standard-8 ...
gcloud compute instance-groups managed rolling-action start-update web-mig --version=template=web-e2-8 --region=R

questions.title: A public address lost while resizing a VM
questions.summary: Changing a VM's machine type requires stopping it, and stopping releases an ephemeral external IP; promote it to static first to keep it.
questions.question: A standalone VM at Ripley Maps has an ephemeral external IP address that partners use, and it needs a larger machine type. What should you do so the public address stays the same?

options.A: Promote the ephemeral external address to static, then stop, resize and start the VM.
options.B: Change the machine type while it runs, so the address is never released.
options.C: Snapshot the VM and create a larger VM from the snapshot.
options.D: Stop the VM; ephemeral external addresses are kept while a VM is stopped.

explanation.summary: The machine type can only be changed on a stopped VM, and stopping releases an ephemeral external address. Promoting it to static first keeps the same address through the stop.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. The promoted address stays with the VM while it is stopped and resized.
option_breakdown.B: Compute Engine changes machine types only on stopped VMs.
option_breakdown.C: A new VM gets a new ephemeral address, so partners would see a change.
option_breakdown.D: An ephemeral external address is released when the VM stops.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud compute addresses create ripley-ip --addresses=CURRENT_IP --region=R
gcloud compute instances stop maps-vm --zone=Z
gcloud compute instances set-machine-type maps-vm --zone=Z --machine-type=n2-standard-8

questions.title: Testing a new setting on Cloud Run without users
questions.summary: Deploying with --no-traffic and a tag creates a revision that gets its own URL but no user traffic, for testing before a switch.
questions.question: The Cloud Run service checkout at Dunmow Shoes serves all traffic from its latest revision. The team wants to try a new MAX_CART_ITEMS environment variable value on a URL only testers know, with no customer traffic, before switching over. What should it do?

options.A: Update the variable; Cloud Run applies it to running instances only for testers.
options.B: Deploy a second Cloud Run service with the new value.
options.C: Update the variable and split traffic 50/50 between the revisions.
options.D: Deploy the change with --no-traffic and a tag, and test the tag's URL.

explanation.summary: A configuration change creates a new revision. With --no-traffic it receives no user requests, and a tag gives it a dedicated URL for testers.

option_breakdown.A: Changing a variable creates a new revision for everyone who follows the latest revision; there is no per-user setting.
option_breakdown.B: A second service works but duplicates configuration and access the team then has to maintain.
option_breakdown.C: A 50/50 split sends real customers to the untested value.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. The tagged revision is reachable on its own URL while customers stay on the current one.

questions.title: Rolling back a bad configuration on Cloud Run
questions.summary: Each configuration change is a new immutable revision, so a rollback sends traffic back to the previous revision rather than editing the bad one.
questions.question: Ten minutes after an engineer at Patterdale Tours changed a Cloud Run service's DB_POOL_SIZE variable, errors spiked. The previous revision, booking-00041, worked fine. What is the fastest way to restore service?

options.A: Send 100% of traffic to booking-00041.
options.B: Edit the variable inside the new revision back to its old value.
options.C: Rebuild and push the container image, then deploy it.
options.D: Delete the service and redeploy it from source.

explanation.summary: Revisions are immutable and the old one still exists, so moving traffic back to it takes effect in seconds without building or deploying anything.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. update-traffic to booking-00041 at 100% restores the working configuration immediately.
option_breakdown.B: A revision can't be edited; changing the variable creates yet another revision.
option_breakdown.C: The image didn't change; rebuilding it adds minutes and doesn't touch the variable.
option_breakdown.D: Deleting the service causes an outage and loses its revisions and settings.

questions.title: Two years of audit logs for the whole organization
questions.summary: An aggregated sink at the organization with children included routes every project's audit logs; the sink's writer identity needs write access on the destination.
questions.question: Security at Ostrander Mutual must query Admin Activity audit logs from every current and future project in the organization with SQL for two years. The logs must land in a BigQuery dataset in the security-logs project, and project owners must not be able to stop the export. Which two actions should you take? (Choose two.)

options.A: Create an aggregated sink at the organization with includeChildren, filtered to the audit logs, routing to the dataset.
options.B: Create a sink in each existing project, routing its audit logs to the dataset.
options.C: Grant the sink's writer identity BigQuery Data Editor on the dataset.
options.D: Grant the security team Logs Viewer on the organization.
options.E: Extend the _Required log bucket's retention to two years in every project.

explanation.summary: An organization-level aggregated sink with includeChildren captures logs from every project under it, including new ones, and project owners can't edit it. The sink writes as its own writer identity, which needs permission to write into the BigQuery dataset.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. One sink at the organization covers current and future projects, and it lives above the projects so their owners can't remove it.
option_breakdown.B: Per-project sinks miss projects created later, and each project owner could delete theirs.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. The writer identity is a service account that must be allowed to create tables and insert rows in the dataset.
option_breakdown.D: Logs Viewer lets the team read logs where they are; it doesn't export anything or give SQL over two years.
option_breakdown.E: The _Required bucket's retention is fixed at 400 days and can't be changed, and a log bucket isn't a BigQuery dataset.

questions.title: Private GKE nodes that can't pull from Docker Hub
questions.summary: Private Google Access covers Google APIs such as Artifact Registry; reaching an internet registry from nodes without external IPs needs Cloud NAT.
questions.question: Halvorsen Media runs a GKE cluster with private nodes in europe-west1. Images from Artifact Registry pull fine, but a new Deployment that uses an image from Docker Hub stays in ImagePullBackOff with a connection timeout. The nodes must keep having no external IP addresses. What should you do?

options.A: Add an egress firewall rule allowing TCP 443 to 0.0.0.0/0.
options.B: Create a Cloud Router and a Cloud NAT gateway for the nodes' subnet in europe-west1.
options.C: Create a new node pool whose nodes have external IP addresses.
options.D: Enable Private Google Access on the nodes' subnet.

explanation.summary: Nodes without external IPs reach Google APIs through Private Google Access, which is why Artifact Registry works. Docker Hub is on the internet, so the nodes need Cloud NAT, a regional gateway on a Cloud Router, to make outbound connections.

option_breakdown.A: Egress is allowed by the implied rule already; the problem is that there is no path to the internet, not a blocked one.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Cloud NAT gives the private nodes outbound internet access in that region without giving them external IPs.
option_breakdown.C: External IPs on nodes would fix the pull, but the stem requires the nodes to stay without them.
option_breakdown.D: Private Google Access reaches Google APIs only, and it is evidently already working since Artifact Registry pulls succeed.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud compute routers create nat-router --network=NETWORK --region=europe-west1
gcloud compute routers nats create nat-gw --router=nat-router --region=europe-west1 \
  --auto-allocate-nat-external-ips --nat-all-subnet-ip-ranges

questions.title: Undoing an accidental DELETE on Cloud SQL
questions.summary: Point-in-time recovery clones a Cloud SQL instance to a moment before the mistake, without losing the changes made since the last backup.
questions.question: At 14:05 a developer at Tolland Pharmacy ran a DELETE without a WHERE clause on a production Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL instance. Automated backups run nightly, and point-in-time recovery is enabled. The team needs the data as it was at 14:04, including the morning's orders. What should you do?

options.A: Clone the instance to 14:04 with point-in-time recovery, then point the app at the clone.
options.B: Fail over the instance to its high-availability standby in the other zone.
options.C: Export the database to Cloud Storage now, then re-import it into a new instance.
options.D: Restore last night's automated backup onto the production instance, overwriting it.

explanation.summary: Point-in-time recovery replays the write-ahead logs onto a new instance up to a chosen timestamp, so it recovers changes made after the last backup. The original instance is untouched while you check the clone.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. A point-in-time clone at 14:04 has the data just before the DELETE, including the morning's orders.
option_breakdown.B: The standby replicates synchronously, so the DELETE is already on it.
option_breakdown.C: An export now would capture the database after the DELETE.
option_breakdown.D: The nightly backup predates the morning's orders, so they would be lost.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud sql instances clone prod-db prod-db-1404 \
  --point-in-time='2026-11-07T14:04:00Z'

questions.title: One set of alerts for fifteen projects
questions.summary: A scoping project's metrics scope can include other projects, so alert policies and dashboards defined once there see all their metrics.
questions.question: Galway Freight runs one service across fifteen projects. The on-call team wants each alert policy defined once, in one place, covering CPU and error-rate metrics from all fifteen projects, including projects added later to that service. What should you do?

options.A: Route every project's logs to one log bucket and alert on log-based metrics there.
options.B: Export the metrics of every project to BigQuery and schedule queries that send email.
options.C: Copy the alert policies into each of the fifteen projects with a script.
options.D: Create a scoping project, add the fifteen projects to its metrics scope, and create the alert policies in the scoping project.

explanation.summary: A metrics scope lets one scoping project read the metrics of the projects added to it. Alert policies and dashboards there can cover all of them, and a new project only has to be added to the scope.

option_breakdown.A: CPU utilisation is a metric, not a log, so log-based metrics would miss it.
option_breakdown.B: Cloud Monitoring doesn't export metrics to BigQuery for alerting, and scheduled queries are not alerting.
option_breakdown.C: Copies work but aren't defined once; each change has to be repeated fifteen times.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Policies created in the scoping project evaluate metrics from every project in its metrics scope.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud beta monitoring metrics-scopes create projects/MONITORED_PROJECT_ID \
  --project=SCOPING_PROJECT_ID

questions.title: Seven years kept, cheap after ninety days
questions.summary: A locked retention policy stops anyone deleting objects early; lifecycle rules change the storage class and delete objects by age without scripts.
questions.question: Hollins Broadcasting stores finished episodes in Cloud Storage. Each object is rarely read after 90 days, must be kept for seven years from when it was written with no one able to delete it sooner, and must be deleted when the seven years end. There may be no scripts. Which two actions should you take? (Choose two.)

options.A: Add lifecycle rules: change objects to Archive at 90 days, and delete them at seven years.
options.B: Enable Autoclass so that unread episodes move to colder classes.
options.C: Set the bucket's soft delete retention to seven years.
options.D: Set a seven-year retention policy on the bucket and lock it.
options.E: Enable object versioning so that deleted episodes can be restored.

explanation.summary: A locked retention policy prevents deletion or replacement of any object before it reaches the retention age, even by owners. Lifecycle rules then do the class change and the final deletion by object age.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. SetStorageClass at 90 days cuts the cost, and Delete at the seven-year age removes each object when it may go.
option_breakdown.B: Autoclass moves objects between classes but never deletes them, so the seven-year deletion would still need a rule.
option_breakdown.C: Soft delete retention is at most 90 days, and it only delays a deletion that someone already made.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Once locked, the retention policy can't be shortened or removed, so nobody can delete an episode early.
option_breakdown.E: Versioning keeps noncurrent copies, but anyone with permission can still delete them; it doesn't enforce the seven years.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud storage buckets update gs://episodes --retention-period=7y
gcloud storage buckets update gs://episodes --lock-retention-period
gcloud storage buckets update gs://episodes --lifecycle-file=lifecycle.json

questions.title: Knowing who reads a sensitive bucket from now on
questions.summary: Reads of Cloud Storage objects are recorded only in Data Access audit logs, which are off by default for Cloud Storage and are enabled in the IAM audit configuration.
questions.question: Compliance at Rowan Legal needs a record, from today onward, of every user who reads objects in the case-files bucket, kept in Cloud Logging. Admin Activity audit logs already show who changed the bucket's settings. What should you do?

options.A: Enable VPC Flow Logs on the subnets the users connect from.
options.B: Enable Data Access audit logs of type DATA_READ for Cloud Storage in the project.
options.C: Nothing; Admin Activity audit logs already record object reads.
options.D: Enable Access Transparency for the organization.

explanation.summary: Admin Activity logs record configuration changes and are always on. Reading object data is a data access, logged only when Data Access audit logs are enabled for the service; for Cloud Storage they are off by default.

option_breakdown.A: Flow logs sample network traffic in a VPC; they don't name the user reading an object through the API.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. DATA_READ audit logs for Cloud Storage record each object read and who made it.
option_breakdown.C: Admin Activity logs cover changes to resources and their metadata, not reads of object data.
option_breakdown.D: Access Transparency logs actions by Google personnel, not by the company's own users.

explanation.gcloud_command: # Console > IAM & Admin > Audit Logs > Google Cloud Storage > Data Read

questions.title: GPU jobs on GPU nodes only
questions.summary: Add a GPU node pool and request nvidia.com/gpu in the Pod's resource limits; GKE taints GPU nodes so that other Pods stay off them.
questions.question: Sorrel Vision runs a GKE Standard cluster whose single node pool has no GPUs. A new inference Deployment needs one NVIDIA L4 GPU per Pod, and the other workloads must keep running on the existing nodes, not on the expensive GPU nodes. Which two actions should you take? (Choose two.)

options.A: Create a new node pool with L4 GPUs attached to its nodes.
options.B: Move the other workloads to Cloud Run so the cluster holds only GPU Pods.
options.C: Attach L4 GPUs to the existing nodes with the gcloud compute instances commands.
options.D: Install the NVIDIA drivers on the cluster's control plane.
options.E: Set a limit of nvidia.com/gpu: 1 in the inference containers' resources.

explanation.summary: GPUs are added to GKE as a node pool with accelerators. Pods ask for GPUs through the nvidia.com/gpu resource; GKE taints GPU nodes and adds the matching toleration to Pods that request GPUs, so other Pods stay on the original nodes.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. A GPU node pool provides the L4 capacity without changing the existing nodes.
option_breakdown.B: Moving workloads off the cluster isn't needed; the GPU taint already keeps them off the GPU nodes.
option_breakdown.C: GKE manages its nodes; editing the underlying VMs directly is unsupported and changes would be lost when nodes are recreated.
option_breakdown.D: The control plane is managed by Google and runs no workloads; drivers belong on the GPU nodes.
option_breakdown.E: Correct. Requesting the GPU schedules each Pod on a GPU node and gives it the toleration for the GPU taint.

questions.title: A BigQuery dataset encrypted with the security team's key
questions.summary: For CMEK in BigQuery, the BigQuery service agent needs Encrypter/Decrypter on a key in the dataset's location, and the dataset's default key is set to it.
questions.question: Security at Penhallow Energy manages Cloud KMS keys in the sec-keys project. A new BigQuery dataset in the EU multi-region of project analytics must encrypt every new table with a key the security team controls. Which two actions should you take? (Choose two.)

options.A: Create the key in the global location of sec-keys so that every region can use it.
options.B: Set the key as the dataset's default Cloud KMS key.
options.C: Create the key in the europe location of sec-keys, and grant the analytics project's BigQuery service agent Encrypter/Decrypter on it.
options.D: Use customer-supplied encryption keys sent with each query.
options.E: Grant the data analysts Cloud KMS Admin on the key.

explanation.summary: BigQuery uses its service agent to call Cloud KMS, so that identity needs Encrypter/Decrypter on the key. The key must be in a location that matches the dataset. A dataset default key then applies to every new table.

option_breakdown.A: BigQuery requires the key's location to match the dataset's, so a global key can't protect an EU dataset.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. With a default key on the dataset, new tables are encrypted with it without each job naming it.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. A key in the europe multi-region matches the EU dataset, and the BigQuery service agent is the identity that uses it.
option_breakdown.D: BigQuery doesn't support customer-supplied encryption keys.
option_breakdown.E: Analysts don't use the key directly, and KMS Admin would let them change or destroy it.

questions.title: SSH to private VMs through IAP
questions.summary: IAP TCP forwarding needs ingress from 35.235.240.0/20 on port 22 and the IAP-secured Tunnel User role for the people connecting.
questions.question: Engineers at Fenwick Grain must SSH to Compute Engine VMs that have no external IP addresses, from their laptops on the internet, without a bastion host or VPN. The VPC has only rules for internal traffic. Which two actions should you take? (Choose two.)

options.A: Create a Cloud NAT gateway for the VMs' subnet.
options.B: Create a firewall rule allowing TCP 22 from 35.235.240.0/20 to the VMs.
options.C: Grant the engineers Compute Network Admin on the project.
options.D: Grant the engineers IAP-secured Tunnel User on the project or on the VMs.
options.E: Give the VMs ephemeral external IP addresses while engineers are working on them.

explanation.summary: IAP TCP forwarding wraps SSH in HTTPS to Google, which then connects to the VM from the 35.235.240.0/20 range. The VPC must allow that range on port 22, and IAM decides who may open tunnels.

option_breakdown.A: Cloud NAT handles the VMs' outbound connections, not inbound SSH sessions.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. IAP's forwarders connect from this range, so port 22 must be open to it.
option_breakdown.C: Network Admin manages network resources; it isn't the permission IAP checks to open a tunnel.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Without IAP-secured Tunnel User, IAP refuses to open the tunnel for the engineer.
option_breakdown.E: External IPs expose the VMs to the internet, which the setup is meant to avoid.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud compute firewall-rules create allow-iap-ssh --network=NETWORK \
  --allow=tcp:22 --source-ranges=35.235.240.0/20
gcloud compute ssh VM_NAME --zone=ZONE --tunnel-through-iap

questions.title: Logs only the security team may read
questions.summary: Route sensitive logs to their own log bucket, keep them out of _Default, and grant access through a log view on that bucket.
questions.question: The payments service at Corriedale Bank writes logs containing card fragments. Those entries must stay in Cloud Logging, readable only by the security team, while developers keep Logs Viewer on the project for every other log. Which two actions should you take? (Choose two.)

options.A: Enable CMEK on the _Default log bucket with a Cloud KMS key that only the security team can use.
options.B: Create a log bucket and a sink that routes the payments logs to it, and exclude those logs from the _Default sink.
options.C: Turn on Data Access audit logs for the payments service so that every read is recorded.
options.D: Grant the developers Private Logs Viewer on the project instead of Logs Viewer.
options.E: Grant the security team Logs View Accessor on a log view of the new bucket.

explanation.summary: Where a log is stored decides who can see it. Routing the sensitive entries to a separate bucket, and excluding them from _Default, removes them from what developers can read; a log view on the new bucket is what the security team is granted.

option_breakdown.A: CMEK controls the encryption key; if Logging couldn't use the key, logging would fail for everyone rather than hide the entries from developers.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. The entries now live only in the new bucket, so developers' access to _Default no longer covers them.
option_breakdown.C: Data Access audit logs add more entries about API reads; they don't restrict who reads the payments logs.
option_breakdown.D: Private Logs Viewer adds access to Data Access audit logs, which widens developers' access instead of narrowing it.
option_breakdown.E: Correct. Logs View Accessor on that bucket's view gives the security team read access to exactly those logs.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud logging buckets create payments-restricted --location=global
gcloud logging sinks create payments-to-restricted \
  logging.googleapis.com/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/global/buckets/payments-restricted \
  --log-filter='resource.labels.service_name="payments"'

questions.title: One hour of access for someone without a Google account
questions.summary: A V4 signed URL grants time-limited access to one object to anyone holding the URL, signed by a service account the requester can use.
questions.question: A customer of Larchmont Surveys, who has no Google account, must download one 2 GB report from a private Cloud Storage bucket within the next hour. Nothing else in the bucket may become accessible, and the bucket must stay private. What should you do?

options.A: Grant allUsers Storage Object Viewer on the object for an hour.
options.B: Copy the report to a new public bucket and send its link.
options.C: Generate a V4 signed URL for the object that expires in one hour.
options.D: Create a service account key and send it to the customer.

explanation.summary: A signed URL embeds a signature from a service account and an expiry, so anyone holding it can read that one object until it expires, without a Google account and without changing the bucket's IAM.

option_breakdown.A: allUsers makes the object public to everyone, and uniform buckets can't grant per-object access anyway.
option_breakdown.B: A public bucket exposes the report to anyone and leaves a copy to clean up.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. The URL works for one object, for one hour, and the bucket stays private.
option_breakdown.D: A key grants everything the service account can do, for as long as the key exists.

questions.title: Which function burns the CPU in production
questions.summary: Cloud Profiler samples CPU and memory use per function in production with low overhead; Trace shows latency between services.
questions.question: After a release, Keld Analytics' Go API on GKE uses three times more CPU per request, though latency between its services hasn't changed. The team must find which functions in the code consume the extra CPU, in production, without a noticeable performance cost. Which tool should you use?

options.A: Cloud Profiler
options.B: VPC Flow Logs
options.C: Cloud Trace
options.D: Error Reporting

explanation.summary: Cloud Profiler continuously samples running code and attributes CPU time and memory to functions, with low overhead suitable for production.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Profiler's CPU profiles show which functions use the extra CPU, in production.
option_breakdown.B: Flow logs describe network traffic, not where code spends CPU.
option_breakdown.C: Trace shows where time goes between and within requests, but not per-function CPU, and latency hasn't changed.
option_breakdown.D: Error Reporting groups exceptions; higher CPU isn't an error.

explanation.gcloud_command:
# In the app: import "cloud.google.com/go/profiler" and call profiler.Start(...)
# Console > Profiler > service api > CPU time

questions.title: A subnet that has run out of addresses
questions.summary: A subnet's primary range can be expanded in place, without downtime, as long as the new range doesn't overlap others; it can't be shrunk.
questions.question: The 10.20.0.0/24 subnet that Ashby Dairy's VMs use in us-east4 is full, and the managed instance group can't add VMs. 10.20.1.0/24 is unused in the VPC and in the connected on-premises network. Running VMs must keep their addresses, with no downtime. What should you do?

options.A: Delete the subnet and recreate it as 10.20.0.0/23.
options.B: Create a new VPC with a larger subnet and peer it with the current one.
options.C: Add 10.20.1.0/24 as a secondary range on the subnet.
options.D: Expand the subnet's primary range to 10.20.0.0/23.

explanation.summary: You can widen a subnet's primary IPv4 range in place; existing VMs keep their addresses, and the new range must not overlap any other subnet or route. A secondary range is for alias IPs such as GKE Pods, not for VMs' primary addresses.

option_breakdown.A: A subnet can't be deleted while VMs use it, and recreating it would mean downtime.
option_breakdown.B: A new VPC means new subnets for the group's VMs and a migration; it's far more work than an in-place expansion.
option_breakdown.C: Secondary ranges serve alias IPs; new VMs still take primary addresses from the full /24.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Expanding from /24 to /23 adds 10.20.1.0/24 to the subnet with no downtime.

explanation.gcloud_command: gcloud compute networks subnets expand-ip-range app-subnet --region=us-east4 --prefix-length=23

questions.title: Keeping BigQuery query costs in check
questions.summary: Partitioning with a filter on the partition column cuts bytes scanned; custom query quotas cap the bytes a user or project can process per day.
questions.question: Analysts at Duncliffe Media query a 90 TB events table, mostly for the last seven days, and on-demand query costs have tripled. Finance wants each query to scan less, and a hard daily limit on the bytes each analyst can process. Which two actions should you take? (Choose two.)

options.A: Switch the dataset to physical-bytes storage billing.
options.B: Create a budget on the project with an alert at 100%.
options.C: Set a custom quota on query usage per day per user.
options.D: Partition the table by event date, and filter queries on that column.
options.E: Add LIMIT 1000 to the analysts' queries.

explanation.summary: On-demand pricing charges for bytes scanned. A date partition lets a filtered query scan only the partitions it needs, and a custom quota stops a user's queries once their daily bytes limit is reached.

option_breakdown.A: Storage billing affects the cost of storing data, not of querying it.
option_breakdown.B: A budget alert notifies, but it doesn't stop queries.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. A per-user daily quota is a hard limit on bytes processed.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. Queries on the last seven days scan only those partitions instead of all 90 TB.
option_breakdown.E: LIMIT reduces the rows returned, not the bytes read, so the cost is the same.

explanation.gcloud_command: bq query --use_legacy_sql=false --dry_run 'SELECT ... FROM events WHERE event_date >= DATE_SUB(CURRENT_DATE(), INTERVAL 7 DAY)'

questions.title: Deploying an image from another project's registry
questions.summary: Cloud Run pulls images as its service agent, so a repository in another project must grant that project's Cloud Run service agent Artifact Registry Reader.
questions.question: Images for Marden Travel are built into an Artifact Registry repository in project build-hub. Deploying a Cloud Run service in project travel-prod from one of those images fails with a permission error when the image is pulled. The repository must stay private. What should you do?

options.A: Copy the image into a new Cloud Storage bucket in travel-prod.
options.B: Grant the deploying developer Artifact Registry Administrator on build-hub.
options.C: Grant travel-prod's Cloud Run service agent Artifact Registry Reader on the repository.
options.D: Make the repository readable by allUsers.

explanation.summary: Cloud Run pulls the container image using the Cloud Run service agent of the project where the service runs. For a repository in another project, that service agent needs read access on the repository.

option_breakdown.A: Cloud Run deploys from container registries, not from objects in a bucket.
option_breakdown.B: The developer's own access isn't used for the pull, and Administrator is far too broad.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. The service agent is the identity that pulls the image, and Reader is enough.
option_breakdown.D: allUsers makes the images public, which the stem forbids.

questions.title: Daily disk backups kept for two weeks
questions.summary: A snapshot schedule attached to persistent disks takes snapshots automatically and deletes them after the retention you set.
questions.question: Rothbury Clinic's three file-server VMs each have a 2 TB data disk. Every disk must be backed up once a day, each backup kept for 14 days and then removed, with no scripts or cron jobs on the VMs. What should you configure?

options.A: A machine image of each of the three file-server VMs, created once every week
options.B: A daily snapshot schedule with 14-day retention, attached to the three disks
options.C: A cron job on each VM that runs gcloud compute disks snapshot every night
options.D: A custom image of each data disk, created every day from the Google Cloud console

explanation.summary: Snapshot schedules are resource policies: attach one to a disk, and Compute Engine takes snapshots on the schedule and deletes those older than the retention period.

option_breakdown.A: Weekly isn't daily, and machine images capture whole VMs rather than scheduled disk backups.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. The schedule takes a daily snapshot and removes each one after 14 days automatically.
option_breakdown.C: A cron job on the VMs is the kind of script the stem rules out, and nothing would delete old snapshots.
option_breakdown.D: Images are for creating boot disks, and making them by hand every day isn't automatic.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud compute resource-policies create snapshot-schedule daily-14 --region=REGION \
  --daily-schedule --start-time=02:00 --max-retention-days=14
gcloud compute disks add-resource-policies data-1 --resource-policies=daily-14 --zone=ZONE

questions.title: Pods and nodes both scaling for a traffic spike
questions.summary: On GKE Standard, the HorizontalPodAutoscaler adds Pods and the cluster autoscaler adds nodes when Pods can't be scheduled; both are needed for a spike.
questions.question: Wymark Tickets runs its web tier on a GKE Standard cluster with a fixed node pool of three nodes. During on-sales, CPU on the web Pods hits 95% and requests time out. The web tier must add Pods as CPU rises, and the cluster must add nodes when new Pods don't fit. Which two actions should you take? (Choose two.)

options.A: Convert the cluster to Autopilot in place before the next on-sale.
options.B: Add a VerticalPodAutoscaler in Auto mode on the same Deployment, also driven by CPU.
options.C: Create a HorizontalPodAutoscaler for the web Deployment targeting CPU utilisation.
options.D: Raise the web Deployment's replica count to 50 permanently.
options.E: Enable the cluster autoscaler on the node pool, with a minimum and maximum node count.

explanation.summary: The HorizontalPodAutoscaler changes the number of replicas from a metric such as CPU. When new replicas can't be scheduled, the cluster autoscaler adds nodes to the pool, within its limits, and removes them when they're idle.

option_breakdown.A: A Standard cluster can't be converted to Autopilot in place; it would mean a new cluster and a migration.
option_breakdown.B: A VPA in Auto mode that also acts on CPU conflicts with a CPU-based HPA, and it resizes Pods rather than adding them.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. The HPA adds web Pods as CPU rises and removes them afterwards.
option_breakdown.D: A permanent 50 replicas wastes capacity most of the time, and three nodes can't hold them.
option_breakdown.E: Correct. The cluster autoscaler adds nodes when Pods are pending for lack of capacity.

explanation.gcloud_command:
kubectl autoscale deployment web --cpu-percent=60 --min=3 --max=40
gcloud container clusters update CLUSTER --node-pool=default-pool \
  --enable-autoscaling --min-nodes=3 --max-nodes=15 --location=LOCATION

questions.title: Alerting on a burst of error logs
questions.summary: A counter log-based metric counts matching log entries, and an alerting policy on that metric fires when the count over a window crosses a threshold.
questions.question: The on-call team at Fallow Couriers must be paged when the checkout service writes more than 50 log entries of severity ERROR in any five-minute window. One or two errors an hour are normal and must not page anyone. Which two actions should you take? (Choose two.)

options.A: Turn on Error Reporting notifications for the checkout service's error groups.
options.B: Create a distribution log-based metric of the latency field in checkout's entries.
options.C: Create an uptime check on the checkout service's public URL that pages on-call.
options.D: Create an alerting policy on it: more than 50 in five minutes.
options.E: Create a counter log-based metric for checkout's ERROR entries.

explanation.summary: A counter log-based metric turns matching log entries into a time series. An alerting policy can then compare the count in a rolling window with a threshold, so occasional errors don't page.

option_breakdown.A: Error Reporting notifies on new or resurfacing error groups, not on a count over a window.
option_breakdown.B: A latency distribution measures response times, not the number of error entries.
option_breakdown.C: An uptime check tests whether the URL answers; it doesn't count error logs.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. The policy pages only when more than 50 errors fall in five minutes.
option_breakdown.E: Correct. The metric counts checkout's error entries over time.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud logging metrics create checkout_errors \
  --log-filter='resource.labels.service_name="checkout" AND severity>=ERROR'

questions.title: Partners who may upload but not read
questions.summary: Storage Object Creator allows creating objects without viewing, listing or overwriting them.
questions.question: Seven suppliers send invoices to Tamworth Foods by uploading files into one Cloud Storage bucket. Each supplier must be able to upload, but not see, list or download any file in the bucket, including other suppliers' invoices. The bucket uses uniform bucket-level access. Which role should you grant the suppliers on the bucket?

options.A: Storage Object Creator
options.B: Storage Object Admin
options.C: Storage Object User
options.D: Storage Object Viewer

explanation.summary: Storage Object Creator contains storage.objects.create but not get or list, so holders can upload new objects and nothing else.

option_breakdown.A: Correct. Suppliers can upload but can't read or list anything in the bucket.
option_breakdown.B: Object Admin gives full control of every object, including reading and deleting them.
option_breakdown.C: Object User includes reading, listing and deleting objects as well as creating them.
option_breakdown.D: Object Viewer allows reading and listing, and no uploads.

questions.title: Proving which rule blocks traffic before sending any
questions.summary: Connectivity Tests analyse the configured path between two endpoints and name the firewall rule or route that blocks it, without sending traffic.
questions.question: A new reporting VM at Ellwood Mining can't reach a PostgreSQL VM on port 5432 in a peered VPC, and the network team suspects a firewall rule or a route. They want to know which configuration element blocks the path without changing any configuration and without needing traffic to flow. What should you use?

options.A: Open an SSH session and run traceroute to the database VM.
options.B: Enable Firewall Rules Logging on every rule and retry the connection.
options.C: Enable VPC Flow Logs on both subnets and wait for samples.
options.D: Run a Connectivity Test from the reporting VM to the database VM on TCP 5432.

explanation.summary: Connectivity Tests, in Network Intelligence Center, model the path from the configuration (firewall rules, routes, peering) and report where and why packets would be dropped, with no traffic sent.

option_breakdown.A: traceroute needs traffic, and Google Cloud's network doesn't answer it in a way that shows firewall rules.
option_breakdown.B: Logging means changing every rule's configuration and needs real traffic to log.
option_breakdown.C: Flow logs record traffic that flows; they need configuration changes and don't name the blocking rule.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. The test names the firewall rule or route that drops the traffic, from the configuration alone.

questions.title: Notebook instances left running overnight
questions.summary: Vertex AI Workbench instances can shut down automatically after a set idle time, which stops compute charges while nobody uses them.
questions.question: Data scientists at Kelso Retail each have a Vertex AI Workbench instance with a GPU, and the billing report shows most of them running all night and at weekends with nothing executing. The instances must stop automatically when unused, without anyone remembering to do it, and keep their data. What should you do?

options.A: Lower the project's GPU quota to zero outside working hours.
options.B: Enable idle shutdown on each Workbench instance with a suitable idle timeout.
options.C: Set a budget alert at 80% for the data science project.
options.D: Delete each instance every evening and create a new one in the morning.

explanation.summary: Idle shutdown stops a Workbench instance after it has been idle for the configured time. A stopped instance doesn't incur compute or GPU charges, and its disks keep the data.

option_breakdown.A: Quota limits creating resources; lowering it doesn't stop instances that are already running.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Instances stop themselves when idle, and the data on their disks stays.
option_breakdown.C: A budget alert notifies; it doesn't stop anything.
option_breakdown.D: Deleting instances depends on people remembering to and loses whatever isn't saved elsewhere.

questions.title: A rotated password that Cloud Run picks up without a redeploy
questions.summary: A secret mounted as a volume that references the latest version is read when the file is read, so new versions are picked up without a deploy; the runtime service account needs Secret Accessor on that secret.
questions.question: A Cloud Run service reads its database password from Secret Manager. The security team rotates the password every week by adding a new secret version. The service must use the new password without a new deployment, and its service account must have only the access it needs. Which two actions should you take? (Choose two.)

options.A: Expose the secret to the service as an environment variable pinned to version 1.
options.B: Grant the service's service account Secret Manager Secret Accessor on the secret.
options.C: Mount the secret as a volume in the service, referencing the latest version.
options.D: Grant the service's service account the Secret Manager Admin role on the project.
options.E: Copy the password into a plain environment variable, and redeploy each week.

explanation.summary: A secret mounted as a volume with the latest version is fetched when the file is read, so each new version reaches running instances without a deploy. An environment variable is resolved only when an instance starts. Reading needs Secret Accessor on that one secret.

option_breakdown.A: A pinned version never changes, so the service would keep the old password after rotation.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Secret Accessor on the one secret lets the service read its versions and nothing else.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. The mounted file reflects the latest version when it is read, with no new revision.
option_breakdown.D: Admin can create, change and delete every secret in the project, far more than reading one.
option_breakdown.E: A plain variable exposes the password in the service's configuration and needs a deploy every week.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud secrets add-iam-policy-binding db-password --role=roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor \
  --member=serviceAccount:orders-run@PROJECT_ID.iam.gserviceaccount.com
gcloud run services update orders --region=us-central1 --update-secrets=/secrets/db-password=db-password:latest

questions.title: Logging charges driven by debug entries
questions.summary: Logging charges by volume ingested. An exclusion filter on the _Default sink drops unwanted entries before ingestion, while audit logs and other entries keep flowing.
questions.question: Cloud Logging charges in your production project have tripled. Most of the volume is DEBUG entries written by containers in a GKE cluster. Audit logs and every entry of severity INFO and above must still be kept and searchable. You want to reduce cost with the least effort. What should you do?

options.A: Disable the Cloud Logging integration of the GKE cluster for its workloads.
options.B: Add an exclusion filter to the _Default sink for container entries below INFO.
options.C: Shorten the retention period of the _Default log bucket from 30 days to 1 day.
options.D: Create a sink that routes the GKE container entries to a Cloud Storage bucket.

explanation.summary: Ingestion volume drives the cost. An exclusion filter on the _Default sink, such as resource.type="k8s_container" AND severity<INFO, stops those entries from being stored, and nothing else changes.

option_breakdown.A: That drops the INFO and higher entries too, which the stem says must be kept.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Only the matching DEBUG entries are excluded before they are stored in the bucket.
option_breakdown.C: Retention up to 30 days is included in the ingestion price, so shortening it saves nothing.
option_breakdown.D: A new sink adds a copy; the _Default sink still ingests the same entries unless they are excluded.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud logging sinks update _Default \
  --add-exclusion=name=gke-debug,filter='resource.type="k8s_container" AND severity<INFO'

questions.title: A single VM that must be rebuilt in another region
questions.summary: A snapshot schedule with a multi-region storage location gives daily, automatic restore points that survive a regional outage.
questions.question: A stateful application runs on one Compute Engine VM in europe-west1 with a 500 GB persistent disk. If europe-west1 becomes unavailable, you must be able to recreate the VM in europe-west4 with data no older than one day. You want to minimize cost and manual work. What should you do?

options.A: Change the disk to a regional persistent disk replicated between two zones of europe-west1.
options.B: Attach a snapshot schedule to the disk that takes daily snapshots stored in the eu multi-region.
options.C: Create a machine image of the VM each night from a Cloud Scheduler job, stored in europe-west1.
options.D: Create a second VM in europe-west4, and copy the files to it with rsync from a nightly cron job.

explanation.summary: Scheduled snapshots are incremental and automatic. Stored in a multi-region location, they remain available if one region fails, and a new disk and VM can be created from them in europe-west4.

option_breakdown.A: A regional disk replicates between two zones of the same region, so a region outage takes both copies.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Daily, incremental snapshots in the eu multi-region survive the loss of europe-west1.
option_breakdown.C: Stored in europe-west1, the images are lost with the region, and the job is extra machinery to maintain.
option_breakdown.D: A second running VM doubles the cost, and the copy scripts are manual work to maintain.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud compute resource-policies create snapshot-schedule daily-eu --region=europe-west1 \
  --daily-schedule --start-time=02:00 --max-retention-days=14 --storage-location=eu
gcloud compute disks add-resource-policies app-disk --zone=europe-west1-b --resource-policies=daily-eu

questions.title: Right-sizing underused VMs with little analysis
questions.summary: Recommender's machine type recommendations are based on observed utilization, so they are the low-effort, low-risk way to right-size VMs.
questions.question: Over the last month, the 40 VMs in your project used on average 15% of their vCPUs, with some short peaks. Finance asks you to reduce the Compute Engine bill without causing performance problems. You want to minimize analysis effort. What should you do?

options.A: Change every VM to a machine type with half as many vCPUs and the same memory.
options.B: Export billing data to BigQuery, and calculate a new size for each VM from its cost.
options.C: Recreate all of the VMs as Spot VMs, which cost much less than standard VMs.
options.D: Review the machine type recommendations that Recommender shows, and apply them.

explanation.summary: Recommender analyses each VM's observed CPU and memory use, peaks included, and suggests a machine type for it. You review the suggestions and apply them, with no analysis of your own.

option_breakdown.A: A blanket halving ignores each VM's peaks, so some VMs would be short of capacity.
option_breakdown.B: Billing data shows cost, not utilization, and building the analysis is the effort the stem wants to avoid.
option_breakdown.C: Spot VMs can be stopped at any time, which risks the very performance problems finance wants to avoid.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. The recommendations come from each VM's own utilization, so they cut cost with little risk.

questions.title: Monitoring an internal service from outside its VMs
questions.summary: Private uptime checks reach internal endpoints registered in Service Directory; the VPC must allow ingress from the uptime checkers' range.
questions.question: An internal HTTP service runs on Compute Engine VMs that have only internal IP addresses. You must be alerted when the service stops responding, measured from outside the VMs, without giving the VMs external IP addresses. What should you do?

options.A: Create a public uptime check that targets the VMs' internal IP addresses directly.
options.B: Install the Ops Agent, and alert when the service's process count drops to zero.
options.C: Create a Cloud NAT gateway so that public uptime checks can reach the VMs from the internet.
options.D: Create a private uptime check through Service Directory, and allow its range in the firewall.

explanation.summary: A private uptime check probes an endpoint registered in Service Directory from inside Google's network, without external addresses. A firewall rule must allow the checkers' source range, 35.199.192.0/19.

option_breakdown.A: Public uptime checks run from the internet and can't reach internal addresses.
option_breakdown.B: A running process can still stop answering requests, and this isn't measured from outside the VM.
option_breakdown.C: Cloud NAT handles outbound traffic only; it never lets probes in from the internet.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. The private check probes the service over internal addresses, and the alert follows from it.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud service-directory services create reports --namespace=internal --location=us-central1
gcloud compute firewall-rules create allow-private-uptime --network=prod-vpc \
  --allow=tcp:80 --source-ranges=35.199.192.0/19

questions.title: Application log files that never reach Cloud Logging
questions.summary: The Ops Agent collects custom log files through a files receiver, and it writes as the VM's service account, which needs Logs Writer.
questions.question: An application on 30 Compute Engine VMs writes its log to /var/log/shop/app.log. The entries never appear in Cloud Logging. The VMs run as a user-managed service account that has no roles. Which two actions should you take? (Choose two.)

options.A: Create a log sink that routes /var/log/shop/app.log into the _Default bucket.
options.B: Grant the VMs' service account the Logs Writer role on the project.
options.C: Enable Data Access audit logs for Compute Engine in the project's audit configuration.
options.D: Install the Ops Agent, and add a files receiver for /var/log/shop/*.log to its config.
options.E: Grant the VMs' service account the Logs Viewer role on the project.

explanation.summary: Cloud Logging doesn't read files on a VM by itself. The Ops Agent tails the file through a files receiver and sends the entries as the VM's service account, which needs Logs Writer.

option_breakdown.A: Sinks route entries that already reached Cloud Logging; they can't read a file on a VM.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. Without Logs Writer, the agent's writes as the VM's service account are refused.
option_breakdown.C: Audit logs record API calls to Google Cloud; they don't collect application log files.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. A files receiver tells the agent which files to tail and send.
option_breakdown.E: Logs Viewer reads logs; it gives no right to write entries.

questions.title: Recovering overwritten objects for 30 days only
questions.summary: Object Versioning keeps noncurrent versions of overwritten and deleted objects; a lifecycle rule on days since noncurrent removes them after 30 days.
questions.question: Applications overwrite and delete objects in the bucket contracts-prod. You must be able to recover any overwritten or deleted object for 30 days, and older versions must not be kept longer than that, to control cost. Which two actions should you take? (Choose two.)

options.A: Add a lifecycle rule that deletes live objects 30 days after they were created.
options.B: Add a lifecycle rule that deletes noncurrent versions 30 days after they become noncurrent.
options.C: Enable Object Versioning on the bucket.
options.D: Change the bucket's default storage class to Archive to reduce the cost of kept versions.
options.E: Set a 30-day retention policy on the bucket, and lock the policy.

explanation.summary: With Object Versioning, an overwrite or delete keeps the old version as noncurrent, and it can be restored. A lifecycle rule on days since noncurrent time removes those versions after 30 days.

option_breakdown.A: That deletes current objects the applications still use.
option_breakdown.B: Correct. The rule counts from when a version became noncurrent, so each is kept exactly 30 days.
option_breakdown.C: Correct. Versioning keeps the previous version of every overwritten or deleted object.
option_breakdown.D: Archive has a 365-day minimum storage duration, so versions deleted at 30 days are charged for a year.
option_breakdown.E: A locked retention policy blocks deletes and overwrites, which breaks the applications.

gcloud storage buckets update gs://contracts-prod --versioning
gcloud storage buckets update gs://contracts-prod --lifecycle-file=noncurrent-30d.json   # daysSinceNoncurrentTime: 30

questions.title: Testing a Cloud Run revision before customers see it
questions.summary: Deploy with --no-traffic and a revision tag: the tag gets its own URL for testing, then traffic is moved to the revision in steps.
questions.question: You are about to deploy a new revision of the Cloud Run service checkout. QA must test the new revision at its own URL before any customer traffic reaches it. After QA approves, 10% of customers should be moved to it. What should you do?

options.A: Deploy with 10% of the traffic at once, and ask QA to test through the service's main URL.
options.B: Deploy normally, and roll back to the previous revision if QA then finds a problem in production.
options.C: Deploy the new revision as a second Cloud Run service, and split traffic between them with DNS.
options.D: Deploy with no traffic and a revision tag, test the tag's URL, then send 10% of traffic to it.

explanation.summary: A revision deployed with no traffic receives no customer requests, and a tag gives it a dedicated URL. Moving 10% of traffic to it later is one update-traffic command.

option_breakdown.A: Customers reach the revision before QA has tested it, and QA can't choose which revision answers.
option_breakdown.B: A normal deploy sends all customers to the untested revision straight away.
option_breakdown.C: A second service duplicates configuration, and DNS weights are slow and coarse to change.
option_breakdown.D: Correct. The tag URL reaches only the new revision, and customers stay on the old one until you move traffic.

explanation.gcloud_command:
gcloud run deploy checkout --image=IMAGE --no-traffic --tag=qa --region=us-central1
gcloud run services update-traffic checkout --to-tags=qa=10 --region=us-central1
